This completes the proof. The general case of SU(2)⊗SU(2)⊗SU(2) has been proved in [8]. The above result can be considered as a corollary of the result of [8] in the sense that (i) the octobit construction O is identical to the sequence of double constructions adopted in [8]; (ii) both the octonionic Möbius transformations defined from the 10-dimensional Lorentz group [10] and those defined in [8] use the nested structure for right/left modules (6), whence they are similar in nature. A question naturally arises that why the operations on the states with four or more qubits cannot be described by the Möbius transformations in higher dimensions. An immediate observation from [2] is that all division algebras can only have dimension 1, 2, 4 or 8, basing on which we can prove the following. 4 cannot be described by the Möbius transformations in corresponding dimensions. Proof First, it has been argued in [5] that for systems with more than three qubits, the state spaces do not have the Hopf fibration structures due to the existence of the zero divisors, and hence do not correspond to any division algebras. Then the Möbius transformations in these higher dimensional spaces can not be represented by the division algebras. In other words, the intertwining transformation matrix G , the counter part of G of the previous proposition, cannot be written as the 2×2 matrix with its components in some division algebra, for if the G exists it must be a 2n × 2n matrix in R n with n = 1, 2, 4, 8, which is impossible for systems with four or more qubits. Hence the diagrams in analogy to those in the above three propositions are not commutative for such systems. These results complete the big picture where the operations on 1-, 2-and 3-qubit states on the (generalized) Bloch spheres can be described by the Möbius transformations with coefficients in the three normed division algebras, C, H and O, respectively. The special roles played by the four normed division algebras in mathematics indicate that these three propositions should also be special for some applications in physics. An application of the 1-qubit case is the antipodal symmetric coherent states defined by the antipodal qubits on the Bloch sphere which in turn can be characterized by the Möbius transformations for symmetric points [12]. In the next section, we generalize this result to the other two cases with quaterbits and octobits.<Symmetric Coherent States>In this section, we discuss the symmetric coherent states obtained by superposing the antipodal qubit states on the generalized Bloch spheres. Here by symmetric coherent state we mean the superposition of arbitary antipodal states on the sphere just as the superposition of the reference state(the north pole) and its antipode. Group-theoretically, these are still the generalized spin coherent states in the sense of Perelomov [13]. Since the Möbius transformations keep invariant the cross-ratios that define the symmetric points, 3 they can be used to transform the spin coherent states to their antipodal symmetric points/states on the Bloch sphere.<Discussion and Conclusion>At first sight one might take this correspondence between qubit geometries and the normed division algebras as another coincidence between different theories. Such coincidences do not always lead to deep insights, except that the coincidental mathematics implies at least the same logical structures of these theories. It has been pointed out in previous sections that the notable appearances of the four normed division algebras in mathematics should correspond to the situations in which the 1-, 2-and 3-qubit states play a very special role. In the last section, we have seen that the Möbius transformations represented by these normed division algebras can be used to construct new symmetric coherent states on the generalized Bloch spheres that are again described by the division algebras. This gives us some confidences that the current correspondence can really reveal something deeper. Let us see some possible connections. First, a celebrated coincidence discussed in recent years is the black-hole/qubit correspondence [16] where many properties of the 3-qubit states can be translated into the properties of the STU black holes in supergravity. But the reasons for these relations are still unkown. In view of the Hopf fibration structures for 3-qubit states, we can speculate that, the topological charges admitted by the Hopf map S 8 S 7 ← -S 15 [17] contribute to the blackhole entropy if the black-hole horizon consists of such topological objects that are added up to give the total entropy, e.g. the monopoles on the fuzzy sphere [18]. If this is indeed the case, theorem 3.3 above denies correspondences for systems with more than three qubits. Second, for quantum computation either the 3-qubit [19] or the 2-qubit [20] gates are shown to be universal. In view of the descriptions of unitary quantum gates via Möbius transformations, we can take the universal quantum gates as the scattering matrices with conformal symmetries. This is exactly the starting point of the integrable quantum computation [21]. We can also first construct the representations of Clifford algebras in terms of division algebras, then, in the spirit of [22], build universal quantum gates via Clifford algbras. The results in this paper present a new understanding of why the universal quantum gates only need to act on 3 or less qubits. To conclude, we have showed that the geometric perspective of the three qubits systems under the action of the LOCC group can be characterized by the octonionic Möbius transformations. This in turn enabled us to show the impossibility of the similar charaterizations for systems with more than three qubits. As an application, we generalized the symmetric coherent states to the three-qubit systems, which is more general than previous results.

Using the QD and geometric quantum discord (GMQD) to quantify quantum correlations, some analytical and numerical results are presented. The results show that, the QD dynamics is strongly related to the number of spin particles N as well as the initial parameter θ of the one-axis twisting collective state. With the number of spin particles N increasing, the amount of the QD increases. However, when the amount of the QD arrives at a stable maximal value, the QD is independence of the number of spin particles N increasing. The behavior of the QD is symmetrical during a period 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π . Moreover, we compare the QD dynamics with the GMQD for a symmetric multi-qubit system in different types of noisy channels.<Introduction>As we all know, quantum correlations such as quantum entanglements, have been recognized as a key resource present in certain quantum communication tasks and quantum computational models [1,2]. Many different measurements of quantum correlations have been proposed to detect and quantify the nonclassical correlations beyond entanglements. Quantum discord (QD), for example, which has been initially introduced by Olliver and Zurek [3], captures more general quantum correlations than entanglements, and later the studies of QD have been vigorously investigated both theoretically [4][5][6][7][8][9][10][11] and experimentally [12,13]. Unfortunately, the evaluation of QD requires a potentially complex optimization procedure in general and analytical results can been obtained only in a few restricted cases of 2 2 and 2 N systems [14][15][16][17][18][19][20][21][22]. In order to avoid the optimization procedure of QD, Dakic et al. [23] introduced another measure of quantum correlations for a more general bipartite quantum systems. This quantum correlation is named geometric quantum discord (GMQD). On the other hand, decoherence is an inevitable phenomenon due to our interest systems interacting with their surrounding environments, which give rise to degradation of quantum systems' coherence as well as entanglements. In other word, the decoherence is a major hindrance to deal with quantum information processing. Hence, it is very interesting and necessary to study the effect of decoherence on the evolution of quantum correlations. Recently the researches on dynamics of pairwise entanglement have been made great progress in various fields [24][25][26][27][28][29][30][31][32]. It has been shown that spin squeezing is relation to pairwise entanglement for arbitrary symmetric multi-qubit states in Ref. [29], where spin squeezing implies pairwise entanglement. Recently, dynamics of pairwise entanglement in symmetric multi-qubit systems is reported by Wang et al. [30]. Yin et al. studied the pairwise quantum correlations of symmetric multi-qubit states by using the geometric measure of quantum discord [31]. Xi et al. investigated pairwise quantum correlations for superpositions of Dicke states [32]. As mentioned above these previous studies, the authors are mainly focused on the pairwise entangled properties of quantum states, and neglect the effect of environmental noise on pairwise entanglement. However, pairwise correlations, as we know, quantified by QD and its geometric measure, in a symmetric multi-qubit system under decoherence noisy channels seem to have been seldom exploited before. Therefor, it is of interest and importance to investigate how the pairwise correlations are affected by decoherence noisy channels. Motivated from the recent study on the dynamics of QD and GMQD under the influence of external environments for different multipartite states [33], such as Werner-GHZ type three-qubit and six-qubit states, we here devote to examining the pairwise quantum correlation properties in terms of QD for pairs of particles extracted from a symmetric state. The two-particle density matrix is expressed in terms of expectation values of collective spin operators S for the large system [29][30][31][34][35][36][37][38][39][40]. In this paper, our attention is mainly focused on what happens to the pairwise QD for a symmetric multi-qubit system in four different types of noisy channels, such as phase-flip, amplitude damping, phase-damping, and depolarizing channels. Using QD and GMQD to quantify quantum correlations, some analytical and numerical results are presented. The results show that, the dynamics of the pairwise QD is strongly dependent on the number of spin particles N as well as the initial parameter θ of the one-axis twisting collective state. With the number of spin particles N increasing, the amount of the QD increases. However, when the amount of the QD arrives at a stable maximal value, it is independence of the number of spin particles N increasing. In addition, the behavior of the QD is symmetrical during a period 2π . Finally, we also compare the QD dynamics with the GMQD for a symmetric multi-qubit system in different types of noisy channels. The layout is as follows: In Section 2, we briefly review the definitions of QD and GQD, and give the expressions of QD and GQD. We illustrate initial states and noisy channels in Section 3. title: Multipartite Fully Entangled Fraction
abstract: Fully entangled fraction is a definition for bipartite states, which is tightly related to bipartite maximally entangled states, and has clear experimental and theoretical significance. In this work, we generalize it to multipartite case, we call the generalized version multipartite fully entangled fraction (MFEF). MFEF measures the closeness of a state to GHZ states. The analytical expressions of MFEF are very difficult to obtain except for very special states, however, we show that, the MFEF of any state is determined by a system of finite-order polynomial equations. Therefore, the MFEF can be efficiently numerically computed.

The analytical expressions of MFEF are very difficult to obtain except for very special states, however, we show that, the MFEF of any state is determined by a system of finite-order polynomial equations. Therefore, the MFEF can be efficiently numerically computed.<Introduction>Quantum entanglement is a crucial ingredient in quantum information processing. In practice, the maximally entangled states are often the ideal resource in many quantum information processing schemes [1,2]. Fully entangled fraction is a definition for bipartite states, which is tightly related to bipartite maximally entangled states, and has clear experimental and theoretical significance [3][4][5][6][7]. In Ref. [8], the analytical expressions are obtained for the fully entangled fraction of any two-qubit states. In Ref. [9] an upper bound of the fully entangled fraction is obtained. In Ref. [10] some analytical results have been derived for some special states. In Ref. [11], the monogamy relations for multiqubit states via the fully entangled fraction have been investigated. Ref. [12] shows that in d ⊗ d (2d ≤ d ) system, there exist mixed maximally entangled states. Based on this fact of Ref. [12], Ref. [13] studies the maximally entangled states and fully entangled fraction in general d ⊗ d system. In this work, we generalize the definition of fully entangled fraction to multipartite case, we call the generalized version multipartite fully entangled fraction (MFEF). Our definition of MFEF is tightly related to the GHZ states. GHZ states are a class of important multipartite entangled states which play vital roles in many experiments either testing the quantum formalism or realizing quantum information processing [2]. The bipartite maximally entangled pure states can be viewed as the bipartite case of GHZ states. Similar to the case of fully entangled fraction, we show that the analytical expressions of MFEF are very difficult to obtain except for very special states. However, we prove that, the MFEF of any state is determined by a system of finite-order polynomial equations. Therefore, the MFEF can be efficiently numerically computed. This letter is organized as follows. In Section 2, we give the definition of MFEF, a lower bound and an upper bound of MFEF, and give the expressions of MFEF for a class of special pure states. In Section 3, we study the MFEF for N -qubit states. title: Effects of Temperature and Electric Field on the Coherence Time of a RbCl Parabolic Quantum Dot Qubit
abstract: We study the effects of the temperature and electric field on the coherence time of a RbCl parabolic quantum dot (PQD) qubit by using the variational method of Pekar type, the Fermi Golden Rule and the quantum statistics theory (VMPTFGRQST). The ground and the first excited states' (GFES) eigenenergies and the eigenfunctions of an electron in the RbCl PQD with an applied electric field are derived. A single qubit can be realized in this two-level quantum system. It turns out that the coherence time is a decreasing function of the temperature and the electric field, whereas it is an increasing one of the effective confinement length (ECL). By changing the electric field, the temperature and the ECL one can adjust the coherence time. Our research results may be useful for the design and implementation of solid-state quantum computation.

Our research results may be useful for the design and implementation of solid-state quantum computation.<Introduction>Quantum coherence [1] (QC) in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) offers critical steps toward many technological applications, ranging from manipulation of qubits in quantum logic gates to quantum devices [2] and nano-switches [3]. Numerous coherent properties (CP) common to ideal quantum systems such as electron spin, quantum entanglement, electron photon interaction have already been demonstrated in various types of QDs. Recent reports have also shown that CP in QD qubit is very similar to that in atomic systems qubit [4] or quantum spin qubit [5]. One of the most prominent issues facing investigation of QC in QDs qubit is the effects of the temperature and electric field on the coherence time [6][7][8][9]. In fact, except for very low temperatures, the time scale of QC is very short, reaching several hundreds of femtoseconds at room and higher temperatures. Our objective in this paper is to show that the coherence time of nanoparticle QD systems can remain sharp and distinct even when the coherence time of the QDs is of the same order of magnitude of those at room temperature and higher temperatures. We investigate the qubit's properties of the QDs using the variational method of Pekar type, and study the temperature effect and coherence phenomenon of qubit. For example, Sun et al. [10] studied the effects of magnetic field on the coherence time of a PQD qubit. Xiao and Wang [11] obtained the effect of temperature on the coherence time of a PQD qubit. Recently, considering QDs of different types of potentials (the cylindrical potential, the hyperbolic potential, parabolic potential, etc.) and various semiconductor materials (GaAs, SiC, RbCl, etc.) [12][13][14][15][16][17][18][19], many investigators studied the qubit properties and the quantum coherence effect. Among different QDs, the RbCl parabolic potential QD is a hot point in the low dimensional semiconductor systems. QDs with parabolic potential is an effective theoretical model for describing real dots, and has been demonstrated by some experimental works [20][21][22]. On the base of the RbCl parabolic potential QD, the quantum coherence time of its qubit in different temperature regions is becoming more and more important. However, the temperature effect of electric field on the coherence time of a RbCl PQD qubit have not been investigated so far by employing VMPT FGRQST. . In this article, based on the VMPTFGRQST, we calculate the temperature effect on the coherence time of RbCl PQD qubit when electrons are in a superposition state, and discuss the effects of the temperature and electric field on the coherence time of a RbCl PQD qubit. According to the quantum statistics theory, the statistical average number of the bulk LO phonons is obtained as where K B and T are the Boltzmann constant and the temperature of the system, respectively. The optical phonons' mean number in superposition state around the electron as follows through ( 8) and ( 9) self-consistently calculation, we can obtain the relationship of λ 0 and λ 1 with the temperature T . From (7) we can see that the coherence time is dependent on the variational parameters λ 0 and λ 1 , so it is connected with the temperature T .<Numerical Results and Discussion>We take the effective mass of RbCl to be 0.432m 0 , and the electron-phonon coupling constant to be α = 3.81 and the energy of bulk LO phonon is ω LO = 21.45meV [32]. Fig. 1 The coherence time τ as a function of the temperature T and electric field F for RbCl crystal and r 0 = 2.0 nm. The solid and dotted lines correspond to the cases of the electric field F = 0.5, F = 1.0, F = 1.5 and F = 2.0 × 10 4 V/cm, respectively. Figure 2 displays the coherence time τ varying the temperature T and the ECL l 0 when electrons are in the superposition state for F = 1.0 × 10 4 V/cm and r 0 = 2.0 nm. The solid and dotted lines correspond to cases of the ECL l 0 = 0.5, l 0 = 0.8, l 0 = 1.1 and l 0 = 1.4 nm, respectively. From the two figures, one finds that the coherence time decreases with increasing temperature. The reason is that the increase of temperature results in the increase of the speeds of the electron and the phonon and then the electron will interact with more phonons. The contribution from the electrons interacting with more phonons, which destructs the superposition state, is relatively strong. And the contribution from the increased electron velocity Fig. 2 The coherence time τ as a function of the temperature T and effective confinement length l 0 for RbCl crystal that makes more electrons to be located on the superposition state is relatively weak. Therefore, the coherence time decreases with increasing temperature, which is in good agreement with the results of Makhlin et al. [33], Wang et al. [34] and Xiao et al. [11], whereas this result is the opposite to the case of asymmetric QD qubit [35]. It also can be seen that the coherence time is an increasing function of the ECL, whereas it is a decreasing one of the electric field. Because the increase in the ground state with increasing ECL is smaller than that in the first excited state. Hence, the energy spacing between the GFES will decreases with increasing ECL, and the coherence time increases. The reason of the coherence time decreases with increasing electric field is that the influence of the electric field in the PQD is stronger in the ground-state than that in the first-excited state with increasing electric field. For this reason, the energy space between the GFES increases with increasing electric field and then the coherence time decreases. The magnitude of the coherence time obtained in the present paper is in the range of 0-100 microseconds, which is in agreement with that obtained in Refs. [36,37], which were obtained individually by experiments and the effective mass envelope function theory. Here one can see that by changing the electric field, the temperature and the ECL one can adjust the coherence time.<Conclusions>The relations of the coherence time of a RbCl PQD qubit on the temperature, the electric field and the ECL are studied by using the VMPTFGRQST. Numerical results show that the coherence time is a decreasing function of the temperature and the electric field, whereas it is an increasing one of the ECL. By changing temperature, the electric field and the ECL one can adjust the coherence time. Our calculated results should be useful for designing the solid-state implementation of quantum computing.

title: Multiple-server Flexible Blind Quantum Computation in Networks
abstract: Blind quantum computation (BQC) can allow a client with limited quantum power to delegate his quantum computation to a powerful server and still keep his own data private. In this paper, we present a multiple-server flexible BQC protocol, where a client who only needs the ability of accessing qua ntum channels can delegate the computational task to a number of servers. Especially, the client's quantum computation also can be achieved even when one or more delegated quantum servers break down in networks. In other words, when connections to certain quantum servers are lost, clients can adjust flexibly and delegate their quantum computation to other servers. Obviously it is trivial that the computation will be unsuccessful if all servers are interrupted.
text: <title>Multiple-server Flexible Blind Quantum Computation in Networks<abstract>Blind quantum computation (BQC) can allow a client with limited quantum power to delegate his quantum computation to a powerful server and still keep his own data private. In this paper, we present a multiple-server flexible BQC protocol, where a client who only needs the ability of accessing qua ntum channels can delegate the computational task to a number of servers. Especially, the client's quantum computation also can be achieved even when one or more delegated quantum servers break down in networks. In other words, when connections to certain quantum servers are lost, clients can adjust flexibly and delegate their quantum computation to other servers. Obviously it is trivial that the computation will be unsuccessful if all servers are interrupted.<Introduction>Quantum computation can solve some computational problems much faster than its classical counterparts. For instance, Shor's algorithms can factor big integers and solve discrete logarithm problems in polynomial time [1]. Grover's algorithm [2] and Long's algorithm [3] for searching problems provide a remarkable speedup over their best-known classical algorithms. Recently, Toyama et al. showed that Long's version is optimal for unsorted database search [4]. Although quantum computation has been extensively studied in theory, the experimental realization is still a great challenge. The current models of quantum computers just allow for several operations on a few qubits, and it is far from building large-scale ones. The first generation quantum computer probably may be put into use in a "cloud" style in the future [5], namely only limited number of quantum computers will be possessed by academia, corporations, and governments and they may play the role of servers, while clients, who only hold classical computers and limited quantum resources or technologies, can remotely access such servers. The privacy of clients is the key in the "cloud" model. It is natural to ask how a client can achieve quantum computation and privacy at the same time. Blind quantum computation (BQC) can offer a solution, since it can allow a client (usually called Alice) who lacks enough quantum technologies to interact with the remote quantum server (usually called Bob) to achieve quantum computation, while preserving the input, output, and algorithm private. The first BQC protocol was proposed by Childs [6] by using the quantum circuit model. But the client Alice must possess quantum memory and have the ability to execute the SWAP gate. Then Arrighi and Salvail put forward another BQC protocol [7]where Alice is required to prepare entangles states and measure them. But It is not universal since it is just employed to compute some random verifiable functions. The first universal BQC protocol [8] was presented by Broadbent, Fitzsimons, and Kashefi (BFK) in which Alice does not need quantum memory or quantum computation power and only requires the ability of generating single qubits [9]. Since then, a series of BQC protocols [11][12][13][14][15][16][17][18][19] have been presented based on various techniques, such as the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) state [15,16], the three-dimensional cluster state [17], the continuous variable [18], and the ancilla-driven model [19]. In the above BQC protocols, the client (Alice) is usually required to own some quantum powers, such as emitting single-qubit states, quantum memory or performing the SWAP gate. In order to make Alice be completely classical, Broadbent, Fitzsimons, and Kashefi modified their single-server BQC protocol to the double-server BQC protocol in Ref. [8], where two servers share Bell states and are not allowed to communicate with each other. Furthermore, Morimae et al. [9] and Sheng et al. [10] ingeniously realize entanglement distillation separately for the double-server protocol even when the two servers are requited to be non-communicating. However, in real life it is rather difficult to keep the two servers from communicating. Therefore, Li et al. proposed a triple-server BQC protocol [20] by using the technique of entanglement swapping, where Alice delegated her quantum computation to three servers who can communicate mutually. Recently, Xu et al [21]. observed that only one quantum server can finish the duties which was assigned to three servers. Actually, since three quantum servers in the triple-server BQC protocol [20] can communicate with each other, it is obvious that one server can get all the information from the other two servers and he can do all the things that the three severs should do. However, the single server is easy to become the bottle neck when large numbers of clients in networks want to implement quantum computation at the same time. It is more practical that multiple servers exist and each of them can implement some operations to reduce the burden of the single sever in large networks. It is crucial that several quantum servers are available when many clients want to start a BQC protocol over the network. However, a few of servers may break down sometimes. In this paper, we extend the triple-server BQC protocol [20] to the multiple-server case, where many clients can still implement BQC in case a few of servers fail in networks. In other words, clients can delegate their quantum computation to other servers if connections to one or more quantum servers are lost. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives a brief introduction to entanglement swapping. Section 3 reviews the triple-and single-server BQC protocols using entanglement swapping in Refs. [20,21] and presents a double-server BQC protocol also through entanglement swapping. A multiple-server flexible BQC protocol is proposed and its security is analyzed in Section 4. The last section concludes the paper.<Entanglement Swapping>As one of the most important quantum methods, entanglement swapping [22][23][24][25][26][27], especially Bell-state analysis which is the key element of it, is rather useful in various quantum communication protocols, such as quantum teleportation [28], secure key distribution [29], quantum secret sharing [30], and quantum secure direct communication [31,32]. Recently, it is also employed in a couple of BQC protocols [20,21]. Entanglement swapping can make two particles that do not share any common past be entangled with each other. This technology is shown in Fig. 1 and can be described as follows: Assume that Alice 1 has a particle a, Alice 2 owns two particles b and b , Alice 3 holds a particle a , the particle a is entangled with b, and the particle a is entangled with b . When we implement a measurement on particles (b, b ) in the Bell basis, the particles (a, a ) will be entangled. In terms of a pair of variables , the four Bell states of two particles p1 and p2 can be expressed as In the triple-server BQC protocol in Ref. [20] and the modified protocol in Ref. [ If we implement a measurement on particles (b, b ) in the Bell basis, the particles (a, a ) will collapse to one of the four Bell states. For example, if the measurement result is (0, 0), the entangled state of the particles (a, a ) is |ψ 0,0 (a, a ) . Fig. 1 The Process of Entanglement swapping<The BQC Protocols Using Entanglement Swapping>In this section, we first briefly review two BQC protocols using entanglement swapping [20,21], and then put forward a double-server BQC protocol also by utilizing entanglement swapping.<The Protocol>In Section 3, we reviewed the existing triple-and single-server BQC protocols based on entanglement swapping, and propose a double-server BQC protocol similar to them. All of them can be used for designing the multiple-server BQC protocol. We propose a multiple-server BQC protocol used in networks in which there are several quantum servers (Bob 1 , Bob 2 , Bob 3 ,. . . ,Bob x ) and plenty of clients (Alice 1 , Alice 2 , Alice 3 ,. . . ,Alice y ). Its pictorial description is shown in Fig. 2. Clients can choose different number of quantum servers and a suitable BQC protocol to carry out the delegated quantum computation according to quantum abilities and quantum resources held by them. Assume one client Alice i who have neither quantum technologies nor quantum resources except that she can have access to quantum channels is going to delegate her quantum computation. At first, Alice i randomly chooses three servers Bob i1 , Bob i2 , and Bob i3 from a network and try to establish connections with them (see Fig. 2a). The specific steps are depicted as follows. (M1) Alice sends requests to three quantum servers randomly chosen from networks. Then three servers return signals to show whether these connections are successful or not. (M2) A trusted center prepares n = (2 + δ)m Bell pairs |ψ 0,0 (B1 k , A k ) , and another n Bell pairs |ψ 0,0 (B2 l , A l ) , where Fig. 2 The proposed multiple-server BQC protocol (M3) According to those signals from the chosen three servers to Alice i , the trusted center and Alice i decide how to proceed. The following four cases may occur. (1) If all connections succeed between Alice i and three servers (Bob i1 , Bob i2 , Bob i3 ), Alice i starts the reviewed triple-server BQC protocol with Bob i1 , Bob i2 , and Bob i3 (see Fig. 2b). (2) If Alice i fails to connect one server, she can implement the proposed double-server BQC protocol with the other two servers. For example, Bob i3 collapses, she can carry out the program with Bob i1 and Bob i2 (see Fig. 2c). (3) If Alice i fails to connect to two servers, she can start the reviewed single-server BQC protocol with the remaining one server (see Fig. 2d). (4) If Alice i fails to establish connections with all three servers, she has to select another three servers from the network and restart the protocol.<Conclusions>In conclusion, we observe that the triple-server BQC protocol can be modified to doubleand single-server BQC protocols since these servers are allowed to communicate with each other. Based on such an observation, we propose a multiple-server protocol which is more practical in networks. Clients who are just required to transmit qubits can use BQC to finish their quantum computation while still keeping the data private. Even if some servers fail in the network, clients can adjust correspondingly and still achieve quantum computation.

title: Asymmetric Bidirectional Controlled Teleportation by Using Six-qubit Cluster State
abstract: We propose a scheme for asymmetric bidirectional controlled teleportation by using a six-qubit cluster state as quantum channel. In our scheme, Alice can transmit an arbitrary two-qubit entangled state to Bob and at the same time Bob can teleport an arbitrary single-qubit state to Alice under the control of the supervisor Charlie.
text: <title>Asymmetric Bidirectional Controlled Teleportation by Using Six-qubit Cluster State<abstract>We propose a scheme for asymmetric bidirectional controlled teleportation by using a six-qubit cluster state as quantum channel. In our scheme, Alice can transmit an arbitrary two-qubit entangled state to Bob and at the same time Bob can teleport an arbitrary single-qubit state to Alice under the control of the supervisor Charlie.<Introduction>Entanglement has been exploited as a quantum resource to carry out different types of quantum information processing such as quantum teleportation [1], quantum dense coding [2], quantum state sharing [3][4][5], quantum geometric computation [6]. Teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state was first proposed by using a Bell state between the sender Alice and receiver Bob [1]. Over the past years, various teleportation protocols have been demonstrated with the help of different types of multipartite entangled [7][8][9]. In 2013, Zha et al. [10] demonstrated that the five-qubit cluster state can be used for bidirectional quantum controlled teleportation. Some different schemes for bidirectional controlled teleportation have been devised using different kinds of entangled states [11][12][13][14][15][16][17]. It is known that the n-particle (n > 3) cluster state is maximally connected with the better persistency than the GHZ state [18,19]. Also the cluster states are robust against decoherence [20]. The four-particle cluster state has some preferences for quantum error correction [21] and quantum computation [22][23][24]. In Ref. [25], it was demonstrated that a four-particle cluster state may be useful in quantum information splitting (QIS) of a single-qubit state and an entangled two-qubit state, and argued it is impossible to split an arbitrary two-qubit state by using a four-particle cluster state. Recently, Nie et al. [26] demonstrated that two four-qubit cluster states can be used to realize the deterministic QIS of an arbitrary three-qubit state by performing only the Bell-state measurements. It is worth mentioning that the six-qubit cluster state has been created in laboratory conditions [27]. Many striking applications of six-qubit cluster state have been found, such as quantum teleportation, quantum dense coding and quantum information splitting [28]. In this work, we present a protocol for implementing asymmetric bidirectional controlled teleportation by using a six-qubit cluster state as quantum channel. Suppose that Alice has two qubits A and B in an unknown state, she wants to transmit an arbitrary twoqubit entangled state of qubits A and B to Bob; at the same time, Bob has a qubit C in an unknown state, he wants to transmit the state of qubit C to Alice. The asymmetric bidirectional controlled teleportation task is completed following the typical procedure that, the receiver applies an appropriate unitary transformation to his qubit, after receiving the measurement results of both the sender Alice (Bob) and the controller Charlie on their separate qubits.<Asymmetric Bidirectional Controlled Teleportation>Now let us present our asymmetric bidirectional controlled teleportation scheme in detail. The schematic demonstration is illustrated in Fig. 1. Our scheme can be described as follows. Suppose Alice has an arbitrary two-qubit entangled state, which is given by and at the same time Bob has a qubit C in an unknown state, where Now Alice wants to transmit the state of qubits A and B to Bob and Bob wants to transmit the state of qubit C to Alice. Assume that Alice, Bob and Charlie share a six-qubit cluster state, which has the form where the qubits 1 and 4 belong to Alice, qubit 5 belongs to Charlie and qubits 2, 3 and 6 belong to Bob, respectively. The initial state of the total system can be shown as where To achieve the purpose of bidirectional controlled teleportation task, Alice and Bob firstly perform a Bell-state measurement on qubit pairs (A, 1) and (C, 6), respectively. Then they announce their results to each other via classical channel. Suppose, Alice's measurement result is + A1 and at the same time Bob's measurement result is + C6 , the corresponding collapse state of qubits B, 2 , 3, 4, 5 are given as Then Alice takes single-qubit measurement in the basis of |± = (|0 ± |1 ) √ 2 on qubit B and conveys her result to Bob. If Alice's measurement result is |+ B , the state of the remaining qubits 2, 3, 4, 5 collapse into the state as And Alice and Bob can co-operate and make a quantum controlled phase gate (QCPG) operation on the qubits 2 (set as a target qubit) and 4 (set as a control qubit). The action of this operation may be described as follow equations: then the state ϕ 2345 will become the following state, If Charlie allows Bob and Alice to reconstruct the initial unknown state, he needs to carry out single qubit measurement in the basis of |± = (|0 ± |1 ) √ 2 on qubit 5 and tells the receivers his result. If Charlie's measured result is |+ 5 or |-5 , then the state of the remaining qubits 2, 3, 4 collapse into the state as or then Bob and Alice need to apply the local unitary operation After doing those operations, Bob and Alice can successfully reconstruct the original state. Thus the asymmetric bidirectional quantum controlled teleportation is successfully realized. Similarly, if Alice and Bob got any other measuring results, with the agreement of Charlie, both Alice and Bob can also effectively recover the original state. According to all the measurement results informed by the others, the appropriate operations which Alice and Bob perform in the last step to gain the quantum information are shown in the Appendix.<Discussion and Conclusion>Now let's us briefly consider the feasibility of this scheme in experiment. It is found that the necessary local unitary operation in the protocol contains QCPG and single-qubit operations, the employed measurement includes Bell-state measurements and single-qubit measurement. It is well known that Bell-state measurements can be decomposed into an ordering combination of a single-qubit Hadmard operation and a two-qubit CNOT operation as well as two single-qubit measurements. Up to now, the progress of Bell-state measurement and the single-qubit unitary operation in experiment in various quantum systems [29][30][31][32] has been reported. In addition, the six-qubit cluster state in our scheme has been reported in experiment [27]. In this paper, we have demonstrated that a six-qubit cluster state can be used as the quantum channel to realize the deterministic asymmetric bidirectional quantum controlled teleportation of a single and two qubit states. In the scheme, Alice may transmit an arbitrary two-qubit entangled state of qubits A and B to Bob and at same time Bob may transmit an arbitrary single qubit state of qubit C to Alice via the control of the supervisor Charlie. We hope that such an asymmetric bidirectional quantum controlled teleportation scheme can be realized experimentally in the future.

title: State Ensembles and Quantum Entropy
abstract: This paper considers quantum communication involving an ensemble of states. Apart from the von Neumann entropy, it considers other measures one of which may be useful in obtaining information about an unknown pure state and another that may be useful in quantum games. It is shown that under certain conditions in a two-party quantum game, the receiver of the states can increase the entropy by adding another pure state.
text: <title>State Ensembles and Quantum Entropy<abstract>This paper considers quantum communication involving an ensemble of states. Apart from the von Neumann entropy, it considers other measures one of which may be useful in obtaining information about an unknown pure state and another that may be useful in quantum games. It is shown that under certain conditions in a two-party quantum game, the receiver of the states can increase the entropy by adding another pure state.<Introduction>Thermodynamic entropy measures the number of ways in which the microstates of the system may be arranged, and it is equivalent to informational (Shannon) entropy which is simply the amount of information needed to specify the state of the system. It may also be understood as a measure of disorder. The problem of information in a quantum system is not of a straightforward generalization of the corresponding classical concept. The two situations are not completely symmetric since in both the classical and the quantum case the observer of information is a classical system. Furthermore, both the sending and the receiving agents of information must make choices, which means that in the quantum case the behavior of the agents cannot be unitary. Von Neumann derived his measure of quantum entropy [1,2], using arguments similar to that of Boltzmann in his earlier derivation of thermodynamic entropy, by counting the different microstates associated with the system. The von Neumann measure of a pure state, even if it is an unknown state, is zero. This latter property is unsatisfactory from a communications perspective because if the sender is sending many copies of an unknown pure state to the receiver, it should, in principle, communicate information. In the classical case, the contents of an entire book may be converted to a single signal by converting the binary file of the book into a number by putting a "dot" before it to make it into a decimal number [3], and if a large number of copies of this signal are sent, the receiver could, in principle, determine its value even in the presence of noise. Likewise, many copies of an unknown pure quantum state can be used to obtain information about the state. Although Shannon entropy is generally used in a communication situation, it is not the only measure of information; other measures with different domains of applicability include those of Fisher [4], Renyi [5], and Tsallis [6]. More recently, Fisher information together with the Bohm's quantum potential has been proposed for quantum information [7,8]. Although the Fisher measure is useful statistically, it is problematic when considered in a communications setting. Thus this information in a Bernoulli process (say fair coin tosses) of n trials is 4n, whereas using our intuition about information it should only be n bits, one for each trial. This paper considers a quantum communication situation in which the sender sends out an ensemble of states to the receiver. It reviews three measures of quantum entropy that may be considered for this situation. These include the von Neumann measure and two more that are inspired by the classical communication entropy of Shannon. Since different sets of mixed and pure states lead to the same density matrix, the actual sets used by the state preparer cannot be determined. We consider the extent that the entropy in a given state can be changed by adding another state to the ensemble with a predefined probability.<Information in Classical and Quantum Settings>In communication theory, information is understood in terms of the yes-no type of decisions that can be made by the receiver upon receipt of the message. It is based on the difference between the a priori and the a posteriori probabilities associated with the messages which implies that their statistical behavior is known. In communication, decision-making occurs both at the source and the receiver. The source must pick a specific message out of the ensemble at each sending instant and the receiver must estimate what was sent since, in general, he operates in a situation of uncertainty due to noise or incomplete information (Fig. 1). The decision making must be non-unitary in the quantum case, since it involves a reduction of the a priori probability. The measure of information is not limited to the probabilities of single messages and it also applies to strings of bits. As more data accumulates, the probabilities between signals (or messages) that are ever more separated in time are revealed. These probabilities can only make sense to the analyzer of the strings, who is the experimenter (or a computer may be programmed to make the estimation). In other words, the consideration of probabilities associated with an experimental scheme that involves senders and receivers posits a mind. Ensemble Fig. 1 The information exchange setting Information is a top-down property and, therefore, to speak of conservation of information [9][10][11][12][13][14] is very different from the conservation of energy, momentum, charge, or other similar quantities that have been traditionally examined in theoretical physics. The desire to see conservation of information as a universal principle parallels that of seeing unitarity as the fundamental transformational mechanism. Conservation of information does not appear to have meaning in the absence of conscious agents. Questions of how the information may be unavailable due to noise [15] or deliberately concealed [16] are also relevant, as is the matter of the characteristics of the physical system processing this information [17]. In the classical communication problem the mutual information between two random variables X (sender's output) and Y (receiver's input) is given by I (X; Y ) = H (X)-H (X|Y ), where H (X) and H (X|Y ) are the entropy values of X before and after the communication has been received. In the quantum communication situation, the Holevo bound [18], [19] tells us the amount of information that can be known about a quantum state. If we fit our problem to the Holevo model, the contribution of the pure state to the information will be zero.<Three Measures of Entropy>The three measure considered here are the von Neumann, the informational, and the composite informational measure. Every density operator may be viewed as a mixture of pure states where λ i are the eigenvalues and |ϕ i are the eigenvectors of ρ.<Ensemble of Mixed and Pure States>Assume that an ensemble of qubits is prepared by a source, S. Let A be preparing specific quantum states for transmission. B, intercepting these states, modifies them by adding further states from an available set. Our objective is to determine how much of a change of entropy can be achieved. Such a situation exists in certain models of quantum cryptography [16]. We assume that A prepares ρ A = λ 0 0 1λ by choosing |0 and |1 with probabilities λ and 1-λ. B estimates the density matrix and then creates a new state by choosing this state with probability 0.5 and another pure state √ (1λ) √ λ also with probability 0.5. Although the density matrix can be decomposed in a variety of ways, the nature of the instruments available for measurement will constrain this decomposition. Indeed, one can imagine that the qubits are produced in a lab and mixed up with the appropriate probabilities they are sent out to the experimenter in the other room to estimate the amount of information in them as has also been investigated in other studies [23,24]. This scenario may also be relevant in certain quantum games.<Discussion>This paper reviews reasons why we may need more than one measure for quantum entropy. It shows that even subsets of ensembles that carry no information have an influence on the von Neumann entropy measure in a manner somewhat reminiscent of interaction-free measurement [25,26]. If science is the game that we play with Nature to find an unknown pure state in some suitable configuration space, then this information (like S i (ρ)) is basis dependent that is obtained by repeated measurements on the ensemble and our discovery of this preferred basis state is the culmination point of science. The paper considered the problem of the decomposition of the single-qubit density operator as a probabilistic sum of pure and mixed component states and although this decomposition can be done in a variety of ways, it may in practice be constrained by the nature of the measurement apparatus available to the measuring agent as may be true in a quantum game. The measure for quantum informational entropy is for communication situations where an unknown pure state can communicate information. It is shown that under certain conditions in a two-party quantum game, the receiver of the states can increase the entropy by adding another pure state.

title: Implementing of Quantum Cloning with Spatially Separated Quantum Dot Spins
abstract: We propose some schemes for implementing optimal symmetric (asymmetric) 1 -> 2 universal quantum cloning, optimal symmetric (asymmetric) 1 -> 2 phase-covariant cloning, optimal symmetric 1 -> 3 economical phase-covariant cloning and optimal symmetric 1 -> 3 economical real state cloning with spatially separated quantum dot spins by choosing the single-qubit rotation angles appropriately. The decoherences of the spontaneous emission of QDs, cavity decay and fiber loss are suppressed since the effective long-distance off-resonant interaction between two distant QDs is mediated by the vacuum fields of the fiber and cavity, and during the whole process no system is excited.
text: <title>Implementing of Quantum Cloning with Spatially Separated Quantum Dot Spins<abstract>We propose some schemes for implementing optimal symmetric (asymmetric) 1 → 2 universal quantum cloning, optimal symmetric (asymmetric) 1 → 2 phase-covariant cloning, optimal symmetric 1 → 3 economical phase-covariant cloning and optimal symmetric 1 → 3 economical real state cloning with spatially separated quantum dot spins by choosing the single-qubit rotation angles appropriately. The decoherences of the spontaneous emission of QDs, cavity decay and fiber loss are suppressed since the effective long-distance off-resonant interaction between two distant QDs is mediated by the vacuum fields of the fiber and cavity, and during the whole process no system is excited.<Introduction>Quantum no-cloning and no-deleting are the inherent properties of quantum mechanics and the basis of quantum information science. It is well-known that the copying and deleting of information in classical computer are inevitable operations whereas similar operations cannot be realized perfectly in quantum computers. The no-cloning theorem [1][2][3] indicates that it is not possible to perfectly copy arbitrary quantum state. And according to the nodeleting theorem [4], it is not possible to delete arbitrary quantum information encoded in a quantum state to a standard one. These ensure the absolute security of quantum communication, which plays a key role in the security of quantum cryptography. It is impossible to clone or delete a quantum state by linearity of quantum theory, so the approximate cloning and deleting of quantum states has become the main objectives of the study in the future. There has been great interest recently on the clone and deletion of quantum states [5][6][7][8]. The approximate quantum cloning [2] including universal quantum cloning (UQC) [9][10][11][12], phase-covariant cloning (PCC) [13][14][15], real state cloning (RSC) [16][17][18], economical phase-covariant cloning (EPCC) [19][20][21], and economical real state cloning (ERSC) [22,23] working without ancillary has been lucubrated. Because quantum cloning has a wide applications in quantum information [24,25], it is very significant to realize quantum cloning. Recently, many schemes for realizing different quantum cloning have been proposed [26][27][28][29][30][31][32], and some experimental realizations have also reported by using different physical systems [33][34][35][36]. With the development of the experimental technology, the physical system used for study of quantum computation and quantum communication are atomic system [37,38], nitrogenvacancy (N-V) center [39,40], semiconductor quantum dot [41][42][43][44][45][46] and so on. In these systems, semiconductor quantum dot [47][48][49][50][51] has unique advantages and practical feasibility in virtue of the excellent scalability and the long coherence time [52] so it has become the most promising candidate to realize quantum information processing and quantum computation. Therefore, it has received wide attention, and some schemes for implementing quantum logic gate and quantum cloning with QD-cavity coupling have been proposed [53][54][55]. For example, Ji et al. [53] proposed two deterministic schemes to implement CNOT and Toffoli gates with the singly charged quantum dots trapped in the double-sided microcavities. And they constructed a quantum cloning machine to copy a quantum state near a given state by using these two quantum logic gates. Yu et al. [54] constructed 1 → 2 UQC, PCC, and 1 → 3 EPCC via quantum dots trapped in cavities. Xiang et al. [55] proposed a scheme to realize CNOT and CZ gates, and to realize a optimal 1 → 2 UQC for electron-spin qubits by using these nearest-neighbor controlled gates. In this paper, we present some schemes to implement the optimal asymmetric (symmetric) 1→2 UQC, the optimal asymmetric (symmetric) 1→2 PCC, the optimal symmetric 1→3 EPCC and the optimal symmetric 1→3 ERSC with the long-range off-resonant Raman coupling between the QDs in separated cavities. The present scheme has the following advantages: the scheme is insensitive to the spontaneous emission of QD, cavity decay and fiber loss because two separated QDs are long-range off-resonantly interacted with each other, and cavity modes and fiber modes are always in vacuum state in the whole operation.<Physical Implementation of the Optimal Quantum Cloning>We consider a QD-cavity-fiber interaction system consisting of two spatially separated cavities connected by a single-transverse-mode optical field as in Ref. [52], with the basic frame being shown in Fig. 1a. Each of three QD spins is trapped in a separated single-mode cavity individually, and the two neighbor cavities are connected by an optical fiber. The interactions between two QDs are controlled by using optical switches S 1 and S 2 . Each QD has a full valance band state |V j and the conduction band states |m x = -1/2 ≡ |0 j and |m x = 1/2 ≡ |1 j . The transition |0 j ↔ |V j is driven by the classical laser fields with detuning L , while the transition |1 j ↔ |V j is driven by the cavity mode with the coupling constant g with detuning c as shown in Fig. 1b. Under the large-detuning conditions, the effective Hamiltonian of QD-cavity-fiber interaction system for QD qubit j and j + 1 can be expressed as [52] where with where ν is the cavity-fiber coupling strength. Under the basis , the evolution operator of the QD-cavity-fiber system is given by Choosing χt = π/2 and performing the single-qubit phase shifts on the j th and (j +1)th QD qubits: |0 → e iϑt |0 and |1 → e i(π+ζ t) |1 , an iSWAP gate is obtained as follows: As described in Ref. [56], two-qubit controlled swap (CS) gate operation can be constructed by using iSWAP gate, that is where The quantum circuit for implementing the optimal quantum cloning by using two-qubit CS gate is shown in Fig. 2, which can be divided into two steps: the preparation and the cloning. The quantum information is encoded on the state of QD1, which denotes the input state to be cloned. The initial input state for three QDs is where α, β are real variables satisfying the normalization condition |α| 2 +|β| 2 = 1 and ϕ ∈ [0, 2π ]. At first, we use three single-qubit rotation operations and two CS gates operation to make qubits 2 and 3 entangle for implementing the optimal quantum cloning, as shown in Fig. 2. After that, the entangled state of 2 and 3 is where After performing the cloning process, the whole state of the system becomes In the follwing, we show how to implement various optimal quantum cloning by choosing different angles of the single-qubit rotations. If we choose the following angles with θ 1 , θ 3 ∈ π 8 , π 4 , we can obtain where which is the optimal asymmetric 1 → 2 universal quantum cloning (AUQC), with the corresponding fidelities being Further, if we choose the angles as the optimal 1 → 2 AUQC can be reduced to the symmetric universal quantum cloning (SUQC) with the corresponding fidelities being ), by choosing the angles where θ 2 , θ 3 ∈ [0, π 4 ], we can obtain which is the optimal asymmetric 1 → 2 phase-covariant cloning (APCC) with the corresponding fidelities are And if we choose the optimal 1 → 2 APCC can be reduced to the symmetric phase-covariant cloning (SPCC) with the corresponding fidelities being . On the other and, if we choose the angles , θ 2 = arccos - we can obtain which corresponds to the the optimal symmetric economical 1 → 3 phase-covariant cloning (SEPCC), with the corresponding fidelities being If the input information state is encoded as |ψ 1 (in) = α|0 + β|1 , with the choice of we obtain which corresponds to the optimal symmetric economical 1 → 3 real state cloning (SERSC), with the corresponding fidelities being<Analysis and Discussion>We now briefly analyze and discuss the experimental feasibility of the present scheme. One of the key issues in the feasibility of a quantum information processing scheme is the relative magnitude of the decoherence rates as compared to the gate-operation time. It is well known that the decoherence of electron spin in quantum dots mainly arises from nuclear spins coupling with the electron spins via the hyperfine interaction, making electron spin dephasing rapid. Its dephasing time for a single electron is estimated to be in a range of 1-100 μs [57]. Recently, however the dephasing time of GaAs electron-spin qubits coupling with a nuclear bath can be extended to more than 200 μs by use of a multiple-pulse Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gillecho sequence [58]. Meanwhile, the relaxation time is about 100 μs for GaAs QD's with 10 5 nuclei [59]. From Fig. 2, the corresponding CS gate requires one iSWAP gate and plus additional four single-qubit rotatins, which can be constructed as (6). The single-qubit gate operations required for implementing quantum cloning in Fig. 1 are realized by classical laser fields [60][61][62], and the electron spin resonance (ESR)-induced rotations have recently been experimentally observed in quantum dots [63]. Each time only the nearest-neighbor two QD spins interact with each other, while the others do not, by turning on and off the optical switches. The interaction time between two QD spins in the cavities is chosen as t = π/2χ such that the two-qubit iSWAP gate operating on the nearestneighbor two QD spins is achieved. Since the iSWAP gate operation is naturally occurring in the interaction between solid-state qubits described by the XY or Heisenberg interaction [64], the iSWAP gate is easy to implement in solid-state systems. And a SWAP-operation has also recently been demonstrated for spin qubits [65]. Based on the presently feasible technology in QD experiments, we can choose g = 0.5 meV, c = 11g, L = 10g, δ = = g = 10.5λ [52,66]. Therefore, the required gate times are t = π/2χ ≈ 2.59 × 10 2 /g and t CS = t + 4t ≈ 0.17 ns, then the total time for implementing the quantum cloning is T = 5t + 20t ≈ 0.85 ns, which is much less than the decoherence time of quantum dots, (here we consider the time t spent in every single-qubit operation of about 10 ps [66]) by using the same parameter relationship of coupling strength and detuning as discussed in Ref. [52]. In our scheme, furthermore, the cloning is obtained with the interaction between QDs, so the infidelity induced by decoherence should be considered in the whole experiment. The same effective decoherence rates due to the spontaneous emissions of QD and the decay of the bosonic modes as discussed in Ref. [52] are κ 0.709 × 10 -5 g and 1.826 × 10 -5 g, respectively. Thus the total infidelity caused by the decoherence is about Next, we will use the optimal 1 → 2 SUQC as an example to discuss the effects of an inexact interaction time between two QDs and a slight fluctuation of the single-qubit rotation angles on the proposed scheme. We assume that the interaction time and the angles of the single-qubit rotations may have a tiny fluctuation from the ideal time, i.e., t int = t ± kt, and from the ideal angles in SUQC, i.e., θ i = θ i ± εθ i (i = 1, 2, 3), respectively, with k and ε being small constants. From the plotting of the effects of k and ε on the fidelities of implementing SUQC in Fig. 3, we can see that the influences of errors on the fidelities of the resulting state are very little. Even when k = 0.20 and ε = 0.04, the fidelity f (k) and f (ε) still can be larger than 0.85 and 0.80, respectively. And we can obtain the similar results by using the same methods in implementing other clonings. In addition, the effect of spontaneous emissions of QDs, cavity decays and fiber losses may not severely affect this scheme since two QDs are long-range off-resonantly interacted with each other, and three spatially separate cavities and fiber modes are always in vacuum fields. In virtue of these properties, we believe that the present scheme is feasible for experimental realization and for implementing scalable quantum communication and quantum computation.<Conclusion>In conclusion, we have proposed an effective scheme to realize not only the optimal 1 → 2 AUQC and SUQC but also the optimal 1 → 2 APCC, SPCC and 1 → 3 EPCC, ERSC for three distant QDs trapped in individual separate cavities connected two fibers. In our scheme, the effective long-distance off-resonant interaction is mediated via virtual excitation of the QDs, cavity fields and fiber fields. When the thermal photons in the environment are negligible, the scheme is insensitive to the spontaneous emission of QD, cavity decay and fiber loss, and during the whole operation neither subsystem is excited.

title: Thermal Entanglement Properties in two Kinds of Two-qubit Spin Squeezing Model
abstract: Using the concurrence (C) criterion, we investigate the thermal entanglement properties in two-qubit spin squeezing model for two kinds of squeezing interaction: one-axis twisting model (OATM) and two-axis countertwisting model (TACM) with a transverse field. To the OATM, in the limit case of T -> 0, the ground state entanglement is initially increased from zero to the maximum value, then decreased in a period of time and suddenly disappeared finally with further enhancing the external magnetic field Omega. One interesting thing is that instead of decaying slowly to zero the entanglement is sudden disappeared with further enhancing Omega or mu (the spin squeezing interaction in X direction), and decreasing the parameter mu or Omega can obviously broaden the scope of entanglement exists. For the finite temperature case, a novelty point is the sudden birth phenomenon occured in the behaviors of entanglement, it is initially to be zero (persists for some time), with further improving Omega and mu the entanglement will be suddenly appeared, and the time interval (persists to be zero) before sudden birth is obviously prolonged with decreasing two parameters. The temperature range of entanglement exists can be extended evidently with increasing mu or Omega, and one can obtain entanglement at higher temperature through changing them. When to the TACM, the ground state entanglement is initially decreased from the maximum value and then suddenly disappeared with increasing Omega. While increasing gamma the ground state entanglement is increased initially from zero to the maximum value and then sudden disappeared with further improving gamma (the spin squeezing interaction in XY plane), proper tuing gamma or Omega can prolong the lives of entanglement evidently. For the finite temperature case, the sudden birth phenomenon also occured in the the evoluted concurrence, the variation of parameters Omega and gamma can reduce the time interval before sudden birth. The influence of the temperature T on thermal entanglement property is also investigated. The temperature range of entanglement existence can be extended evidently with increasing gamma, one can obtain entanglement at higher temperature through changing parameters gamma and Omega.

Due to its potential applications, In recent years, there has been an ongoing effort to study and characterize qualitatively the entanglement properties of condensed matter systems, and apply them in quantum information. When QIP comes to generation, the temperature should be considered since in most cases the thermal fluctuation can result in disentanglement. Since the entanglement is fragile, the problem of how to create stable entanglement remains a main focus of recent studies in the field of quantum information processing. The thermal entanglement, which differs from the other kind of entanglement by its advantages of stability, requires neither measurement nor controlled switching of interactions in the preparation process, therefore the thermal entanglement in various systems is an attractive topic and worth intensively studying [4,5]. To be one kind of fundamental entanglement generation resource, the thermal entanglement in solid state systems such as spin chains is an important emerging field [6,7]. The Heisenberg chain, the simplest spin chain, has been used to construct a quantum computer [8,9]. In Ref. [10], the concept of thermal entanglement in solids was introduced and studied in a one-dimensional anisotropic Heisenberg model. Thermal entanglement in two qubits Heisenberg XX chains was investigated with and without an external magnetic field [11]. The thermal entanglement also has been extensively studied for various systems including isotropic Heisenberg chain [12,13], anisotropic Heisenberg chain [14], Ising model in an arbitrarily directed magnetic field [15], and cavity-QED [16] since the seminal works by Arnesen and Nielsen [17]. The effects of anisotropy, inhomogeneous field and the interaction of Z-component J z have also been studied in a lot of works for different kinds of Heisenberg models [4,7,18]. However, it is little researched the entanglement properties in various spin squeezing models, and it can imply us some new control parameters on entanglement. Therefore, in this paper, we investigate the properties of thermal entanglement in two kinds of Two-qubit spin squeezing models with uniform magnetic field. title: Processes of Quantum Associative Memory (QuAM) Through New Maximally Entangled States (Singh-Rajput MES)
abstract: Using Singh-Rajput MES as memory states in the evolutionary process of pattern storage and the non-evolutionary process of pattern recall (the two fundamental constituents of QuAM), the suitability and superiority of these MES over Bell's MES have been demonstrated in both these processes. It has been shown that, under the operations of all the possible memorization operators for a two-qubit system, the first two states of Singh-Rajput MES are useful for storing the pattern |11 > and the last two of these MES are useful in storing the pattern |10 > while Bell's MES are not much suitable as memory states in a valid memorization process. The recall operations have also been conducted by separately choosing Singh-Rajput MES and Bell's MES as memory states for possible various queries and it has been shown that in each case the choices of Singh-Rajput MES as valid memory states are much more suitable than those of Bell's MES.

It has been shown that, under the operations of all the possible memorization operators for a two-qubit system, the first two states of Singh-Rajput MES are useful for storing the pattern |11 > and the last two of these MES are useful in storing the pattern |10 > while Bell's MES are not much suitable as memory states in a valid memorization process. The recall operations have also been conducted by separately choosing Singh-Rajput MES and Bell's MES as memory states for possible various queries and it has been shown that in each case the choices of Singh-Rajput MES as valid memory states are much more suitable than those of Bell's MES.<Introduction>In last fifteen years quantum entanglement [1] has played important role in the fields of quantum information theory [2,3], quantum computers [4], universal quantum computing network [5], teleportation [6], dense coding [7,8], geometric quantum computation [9,10] and quantum cryptography [11][12][13]. The simplest non-trivial multi-particle system that can be investigated theoretically, as well as experimentally, consists of two qubits which display many of the paradoxical features of quantum mechanics such as superposition and entanglement. Basis of entanglement is the correlation that can exist between qubits. From physical point of view, entanglement is still little understood. What makes it too powerful is the fact that since quantum states exist as superposition, these correlations exist in superposition as well and when superposition is destroyed, the proper correlation is somehow communicated between the qubits [14]. It is this communication that is the crux of entanglement. Entanglement is one of the key resources required for quantum computation and hence the experimental creation and measurement of entangled states is of crucial importance for various physical implementations of quantum computers. The generation of quantum entanglement among spatially separated particles requires non-local interactions through which the quantum correlations are dynamically created [15] but our present knowledge of quantum entanglement is not at all satisfactory [16]. However, the functional dependence of the entanglement measures like concurrence [17,18], i-concurrence [19] and 3-tangle [20] on spin-correlation functions have been established [21]. Recent papers concerning entanglement in quantum-spin systems address the questions about the maximum entanglement of nearest neighbour qubits belonging to a ring of qubits in a translational invariant quantum state [22], the dependence of entanglement between two qubits on temperature and external magnetic field [23][24][25], three-qubits XYZ-model [26,27] and XY-model [28]. Quantum Associative Memory (QuAM) is an important tool for pattern recognition, intelligent control and artificial intelligence. Ventura and Martinez have built [29] QuAM where the stored patterns are considered as the basis states of the memory quantum states. They used a modified version of well known Grover's quantum search algorithm [3] in an unsorted database as the retrieval algorithm. To overcome the limits of this model to only solve the completion problem by doing data retrieving from the noisy data, Ezhov et al have used [5,30] an exclusive method of quantum superposition and Grover's algorithm [3] with distributed queries. QuAM is the most promising approach to completion process and it incorporates pattern association which consist of two very important processes: Pattern Storage (or Memorization) and Pattern Recall. Primary purpose of QuAM is to memorize a set of patterns for completion and it has the ability to generalize over patterns not seen during learning. Such quantum approach to associative memory is the ability to provide for storage capabilities up to the order of 2 m in a m-qubit circuit (i.e. storage of four states in a two qubit system). Another benefit of quantum associative scheme worth mentioning is the fact that it provides the natural setting for considering higher order bit patterns. In the process of storage constituent of QuAM, a coherent superposition of states is created that corresponds to the pattern where the amplitude of states in the superposition are all equal. In QuAM the quantum effects of coherence, interference and entanglement make the exponential storage capacity possible. Thus QuAM can store an exponential number of memories and retrieve them in sub-exponential time [31]. General form of QuAM suggests that the database includes all basis states but some of them are not used and correspond to spurious memories. In our very recent paper [32] a new set of maximally entangled states (Singh-Rajput MES) constituting a very powerful and reliable eigen basis (Singh-Rajput Basis) (different from Bell's magic bases) of two-qubit systems has been constructed, the functional dependence of the entanglement measures on spin correlation functions has been established in terms of these MES, and the suitability and superiority of these MES, over Bell's MES [18], for pattern classification in a two-qubit system, have been demonstrated [33,34]. In the present paper we have used Singh-Rajput MES as memory states in the evolutionary process of pattern storage and the non-evolutionary process of pattern recall (the two fundamental constituents of QuAM) and demonstrated the suitability of these MES over Bell's MES. Carrying out the storage element of QuAM by applying all possible memorizing operators for a two qubit system on Singh-Rajput MES one by one, the corresponding sets of modified memorized states have been obtained and it has been demonstrated that under the operations of all the possible memorization operators for a two-qubit system the first two states of Singh-Rajput MES are useful for storing the pattern |11 > and the last two of these MES are useful in storing the pattern |10 > . The recall operations of quantum associate memory (QuAM), for a two-qubit system, have been conducted through non-evolutionary processes in terms of non-unitary operators by separately choosing our recently derived maximally entangled states (Singh-Rajput MES) and Bell's MES as memory states for various queries and it has been shown that in each case the choices of Singh-Rajput MES as valid memory states are much more suitable than those of Bell's MES.<Pattern Storage in QuAM Through Singh-Rajput MES>The algorithm for constructing a coherent state over n qubits to represent a set of m patterns is implemented using a polynomial number ( in length and the number of patterns) of elementary operations over qubits. The key operator in this process (memorization operator) is [29] where m ≥ p ≥ 1. This evolutionary nature of storing process is necessary for the system to maintain coherent superposition that represents the stored patterns. For n=4 in a two qubit system the nine states are required first four of which constitute four maximally entangled states ( Singh-Rajput MES) and the remaining five are their transformations after each iteration.
