title: Quantum Discord Preservation for Two Quantum-Correlated Qubits in Two Independent Reserviors
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of quantum discord using an exactly solvable model where two qubits coupled to independent thermal environments. The quantum discord is employed as a non-classical correlation quantifier. By studying the quantum discord of a class of initial states, we find discord remains preserve for a finite time. The effects of the temperature, initial-state parameter, system-reservoir coupling constant and temperature difference parameter of the two independent reserviors are also investigated. We discover that the quantum nature loses faster in high temperature, however, one can extend the time of quantum nature by choosing smaller system-reservoir coupling constant, larger certain initial-state parameter and larger temperature difference parameter.
text: <title>Quantum Discord Preservation for Two Quantum-Correlated Qubits in Two Independent Reserviors<abstract>We investigate the dynamics of quantum discord using an exactly solvable model where two qubits coupled to independent thermal environments. The quantum discord is employed as a non-classical correlation quantifier. By studying the quantum discord of a class of initial states, we find discord remains preserve for a finite time. The effects of the temperature, initial-state parameter, system-reservoir coupling constant and temperature difference parameter of the two independent reserviors are also investigated. We discover that the quantum nature loses faster in high temperature, however, one can extend the time of quantum nature by choosing smaller system-reservoir coupling constant, larger certain initial-state parameter and larger temperature difference parameter.<Introduction>Since quantum entanglement is consumed during operation [1][2][3][4][5][6][7], it is required to know whether the quantum entanglement contained in a number of quantum systems is sufficient to perform a certain computational task. Actually, quantum entanglement is a distinctive quantum feature of correlations, but not the only one. In order to capture nonclassical correlations, several measures of correlations have been proposed in the literature [8][9][10][11][12][13][14], among them, quantum discord has received considerable attention [15][16][17][18][19][20][21], which quantifies the quantumness of correlations between partitions A and B of a composite state [22]. Quantum discord is defined as the mismatch between two quantum analogs of classically equivalent expression of the mutual information, which measures general nonclassical correlations, including entanglement. For pure entangled states, all nonclassical correlations characterized by quantum discord are identified as entanglement. For mixed states, the entanglement only partly describes nonclassical correlation. Even for some separable states, although there is no entanglement between these two parts, the quantum discord is nonzero [23], nonzero values of discord indicate the presence of nonclassical correlations. And compared to classical counterparts, such separable states can also improve performance in some computational tasks [24,25]. Moreover, quantum discord is more robust than the entanglement against decoherence [26][27][28][29]. Also, unlike the entanglement, which exhibits sudden death [30][31][32][33][34][35][36], the quantum discord displays the phenomenon of sudden change [37]. The existence of a finite time interval during which quantum discord preserves, subsequently, quantum discord starts to decay at a critical time point t c [38]. Therefore, how to extend the critical time t c will be of significant importance for communication and information processing. Any realistic quantum system is inevitably interacting with the surrounding thermal environment, which causes the rapid destruction of crucial quantum properties. Therefore, besides the characterization and quantification of correlations, an interesting and crucial issue is the behavior of correlations under the action of decoherence. Researches on dynamics of the quantum discord have been widely studied by using models where qubits interacts in a common zero-temperature reservoir [21,29,39]. Is it possible to preserve discord for a interval that is long enough to perform quantum computation or communication in two independent thermal environments by adjusting the parameters of system and environments? In this paper, the bipartite correlations is investigated via a microscopic model where two qubits coupled to its independent environments at finite temperatures. We study the dynamics of both quantum and classical correlations under the noisy environments. By analytically calculating the dynamic evolution of the system under our consideration, we find that each noisy environment constructs an independent non-dissipative channel for each corresponding qubit due to energy exchange between qubits and environments. Quantum discord is employed as a measure of quantum correlation. Through discussing the quantum discord of a class of initial states, a sudden change of quantum discord in the evolution is found, which allows us to define a critical time t c . Before the critical time, quantum discord preserves a constant. And after t c , it starts to decay. The influence of the temperature on the quantum discord is investigated, showing quantum nature loses faster when the reservoir is in high temperature. However, the quantum nature can preserve longer by choosing smaller system-reservoir coupling constant, larger certain initial-state parameter and larger temperature difference parameter. This paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we present our physical model and study its time evolution. In Section 3, we investigate dynamical behaviors of quantum discord for a given initial state. The effects of the temperature, the initial-state parameters, the systemreservoir coupling constant and the temperature difference parameter of two independent reserviors on the quantum discord are studied in Section 4. We summarize our conclusion at the end of this paper.<The Model and its Evolution>The total system we consider is consist of a pair of noninteracting two-level atoms A and B in heat bath 1 and 2, respectively. The energy separation between the excited |e and ground state |g of atoms is denoted by i (i = A, B). Atoms A and B are coupled individually to its thermal bath with temperature T a and T b , respectively. Here, each bath is modeled as an infinite number of harmonic oscillators with frequencies ω ak and ω bk , which couple to the relevant electronic degrees of freedom of atom i via the coupling constants g ik . title: Optimizing Teleportation Cost in Distributed Quantum Circuits
abstract: The presented work provides a procedure for optimizing the communication cost of a distributed quantum circuit (DQC) in terms of the number of qubit teleportations. Because of technology limitations which do not allow large quantum computers to work as a single processing element, distributed quantum computation is an appropriate solution to overcome this difficulty. Previous studies have applied ad-hoc solutions to distribute a quantum system for special cases and applications. In this study, a general approach is proposed to optimize the number of teleportations for a DQC consisting of two spatially separated and long-distance quantum subsystems. To this end, different configurations of locations for executing gates whose qubits are in distinct subsystems are considered and for each of these configurations, the proposed algorithm is run to find the minimum number of required teleportations. Finally, the configuration which leads to the minimum number of teleportations is reported. The proposed method can be used as an automated procedure to find the configuration with the optimal communication cost for the DQC. This cost can be used as a basic measure of the communication cost for future works in the distributed quantum circuits.
text: <title>Optimizing Teleportation Cost in Distributed Quantum Circuits<abstract>The presented work provides a procedure for optimizing the communication cost of a distributed quantum circuit (DQC) in terms of the number of qubit teleportations. Because of technology limitations which do not allow large quantum computers to work as a single processing element, distributed quantum computation is an appropriate solution to overcome this difficulty. Previous studies have applied ad-hoc solutions to distribute a quantum system for special cases and applications. In this study, a general approach is proposed to optimize the number of teleportations for a DQC consisting of two spatially separated and long-distance quantum subsystems. To this end, different configurations of locations for executing gates whose qubits are in distinct subsystems are considered and for each of these configurations, the proposed algorithm is run to find the minimum number of required teleportations. Finally, the configuration which leads to the minimum number of teleportations is reported. The proposed method can be used as an automated procedure to find the configuration with the optimal communication cost for the DQC. This cost can be used as a basic measure of the communication cost for future works in the distributed quantum circuits.<Introduction>Quantum computation [1] is an emerging field of study with great potential to outperform classical computers in certain problems such as integer factorization [2], discrete logarithm finding, and database search [3]. Despite the theoretical advantages of quantum computations, realization of a large-scale quantum system is a real challenge [4]. It is mainly because that quantum computation technologies have limitations in the number of qubits they can process [5] and building a large-capacity quantum computer is hard [6] which makes distributed implementations of quantum technologies necessary [7]. One of the limitations of quantum implementations is due to the interactions of qubits with the environment that leads to the decoherence and when the number of qubits increases, the quantum information becomes more fragile and more susceptible to errors [8]. To overcome the mentioned problems, using distributed nodes or subsystems in a quantum system is a reasonable solution in which fewer qubits are used in each node or subsystem. Therefore, to have a large quantum computer, one appropriate solution is to build a network of limited-capacity quantum computers which are interconnected through a quantum or classical channel and altogether can implement the behavior of the whole quantum system [9]. This structure is known as distributed quantum computer. In order to perform a distributed quantum computation, there should be a reliable mechanism for communication between separate nodes of a distributed quantum system. Long-distance quantum communication is a technological challenge for physical realizations of quantum communication [10]. In this regard, teleportation [11] is a primitive protocol for such this communication that uses entangled qubits to distribute quantum information [12]. This protocol has been experimentally implemented in many quantum technologies such as quantum photonics [13], NMR [14], and trapped ions [15]. In teleportation, qubit states are teleported from one node to another, without physically moving them and then computations are performed locally on qubits, which is also known as teledata. There is an alternative approach, called telegate that executes gates remotely using the teleported gate approach without the need for qubits to be nearby [16]. For some applications, like some adder algorithms it has been shown that teledata outperforms telegate and also its performance is independent of the network topology [17]. In this study, teledata is considered for communication between distributed nodes. Teleportation is a costly operation in a distributed quantum system. Moreover, according to no-cloning theorem [18], when a qubit is teleported to a destination subsystem, it can no longer be used in its own subsystem. Therefore, minimizing the number of teleportations in a distributed quantum system is an important concern. In this study, this problem is considered and an algorithm is presented to optimize the number of teleportations for a distributed quantum system consisting of two spatially separated and long-distance quantum subsystems. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 explains some basic concepts and definitions of quantum computation and distributed quantum computing. Related work is presented in Section 3. Section 4 then establishes some definitions and notation needed for the proposed algorithm. Our proposed algorithm for optimal distributed quantum circuit is described in Section 5. Finally in Section 6, we conclude the paper.<Background>A generic scenario for a distributed quantum computation consists of n nodes in a quantum network. These nodes agree on performing a given computation by using a distributed quantum circuit (DQC). A DQC consists of n limited capacity quantum circuits or partitions which are located far from each other and altogether emulate the functionality of a large quantum circuit. Partitions of a DQC communicate by sending their qubits to each other using a specific quantum communication channel through teleportation. In this study, it is assumed that data transfer between distributed nodes in the system is performed by teleportation. Teleportation allows us to send the state of a qubit from point A to point B by communicating only two classical bits. To complete this task, the sender and the receiver at the beginning need to share a maximal entangled state which serves as the quantum channel. Figure 1 shows the quantum circuit for a basic quantum teleportation as described in [1]. In this figure, the two top lines represent the sender's system and the bottom line is the receiver's one. The meters represent measurement, and the double lines coming out of them carry classical bits. As stated in [11] and mathematically proved in [6], it can be concluded that teleporting a quantum state works even if that state is a mixed or an entangled state and so it can be used as communication protocol between distributed quantum systems. The quantum channel connecting A and B is considered to be maximally entangled in order to achieve faithful teleportation. However, due to interactions with the environment, an entangled state may lose its coherence and become a mixed one, which reduces the efficiency of the protocol. Therefore, in order to obtain secure teleportation, the noisy quantum channel should be fixed using some approaches including quantum distillation [19] or by using weak measurement to improve the fidelity of teleportation via noisy channels [20].<Related Work>Distributed quantum computing has been studied for more than fifteen years [6] and the first suggestions were made by Grover [21], Cleve and Buhrman [22] and later by Cirac et al., [23]. In [21], Grover presented a distributed quantum system where there are some particles at remote locations and each one performs its computation and sends the required information to a base station when necessary. He mentioned that the issue in distributed quantum computing is how to optimally divide the problem into the different quantum computing units. The answer to this question effects the performance of the proposed problem in this work that can be considered in the future. Grover showed that using this distributed approach, the overall computation time is faster proportional to the number of such distributed particles. In the same paper, he also presented a quantum algorithm and adapted it to distributed computation where communication is costly. Beals et al. [24] provided some algorithms for efficiently moving and addressing quantum memory in parallel. This imply that the quantum circuit model can be simulated with a Fig. 1 Quantum circuit for teleporting a qubit [1] low overhead by a distributed quantum computer with nodes connected using a hypercube graph. Yepez [25] presented an architecture for distributed quantum computing with two types of communication which were called type I and type II. Type I quantum computer uses quantum communication between subsystems and type II quantum computer exploits classical communication between subsystems of the distributed computer. Using this classification, our distributed quantum circuit is of type I. Related to teleportation cost, Streltsov et al., [26] posed the question of the cheapest way for distributing entanglement and provided the minimal quantum cost for sending an entangled composite state in a long distance. They showed that regarding the most general distribution protocol, the amount of entanglement sent in the total process of distributed communication cannot be larger than the total entanglement cost for sending the ancilla particle and sending back that particle. Classical communication cost is the subject of the study in [27]. Authors conjecture that in a two-stage teleportation, each step requires a single bit of classical communication and in general, for an arbitrary N -dimensional pure state, 2log 2 N bits of classical communication is required for remote preparation which is different from the usual teleportation in which the precise state of the qubit to be prepared in the receiver is known to the sender. Ying and Feng [6] provided some definitions of a distributed quantum computing system and defined an algebraic language to describe quantum circuits for distributed quantum computing. Van Meter et al., [16] designed a fixed distributed quantum circuit for VBE carry-ripple adder. They evaluated the cost of the teleportation for the designed distributed system. They compared two approaches, namely teledata and telegate topologies of quantum circuits and showed that teleportation of data (the one we use in our work) is better than teleportation of gates. They also compared it to a monolithic machine and showed that as the node sizes are increased the multicomputer architecture has better performance in large problem sizes. But their distributed quantum circuit was a predesigned architecture and they did not make any specific change in the system to reduce the number of teleportation circuits in the design. Also in [28], authors used the teleportation communication model for implementing a distributed version of Shor's algorithm. But like the one in [29], their method for assigning logical qubits to distributed nodes is an ad-hoc method specific for implementing Shor's algorithm. In their implementation, each computing node holds n/4 qubits from each register and output of each computing node is teleported to the next computing node. So there is no optimization in the number of teleportations and also the authors did not consider the cost of returning the teleported qubits back into their own subsystems. In [30,31], the path through scalable quantum computers using distributed-memory multicomputer architectures is considered.<Definitions and Notations>In this section, we establish some assumptions and notations before proceeding with the main development of the study. First of all, we assume that there is a quantum circuit, QC as input with width W , size S, and depth D with the following definitions as stated in [32]: The width of a quantum circuit is defined as the total number of qubits in the circuit. The size of a quantum circuit is the total number of its gates from a set of universal quantum gates. The depth of a quantum circuit is the number of timesteps, D required for executing the circuit. In each timestep one or more gates can be executed in parallel. It is assumed that there is an appropriate ordering of gate executions in the sense the number of timesteps is minimal. In each timestep, a set of gates that can be performed in parallel are executed. For simplicity, in this paper it is assumed that there are just two partitions in DQC, each with the size of W/2. Without losing the generality, W is assumed to be an even number. Qubits are numbered from top to bottom from one to n in each partition, where the i th line of the circuit from top to bottom represents the i th qubit, q i . The gates are numbered in order of their executions in the QC and g i means the i th gate which is executed according to a scheduling algorithm. For gates which can be executed in parallel, the priority of their numbering is arbitrary. The set of all gates in the circuit is represented by G. There are three kinds of quantum gates in the DQC, namely, single-qubit, local and global CNOT gates and their definitions and representations are as follows: -A single-qubit gates is shown as gate name i (p, j ). p, indicates the index of partition to which the gate gate name i belongs and j indicates the index of the qubit the gate acts on. -A local CNOT gate is the one whose control and target qubits belong to the same partition and is shown as CNOT i (p, j c , j t ). p indicates the index of partition to which the gate CNOT i belongs. j c (j t ) indicates the index of control (target) qubit in its partition. -Aglobal CNOT gate is the one whose control and target qubits belong to different partitions is called a global CNOT gate shown as CNOT i (p c , j c , p t , j t ). j c (j t ) indicates the index of control (target) qubit in its home partition. The partition to which each qubit q of a global CNOT gate belongs is called the home partition of q. p c (p t ) indicates the index of partition to which the control (target) of CNOT i belongs. It is supposed that local gates including single-qubit and local CNOT gates are performed in their local partitions. The total number of gates in a QC and the number of global gates are denoted by m t and m g respectively. Also a subset of G for representing the set of global gates is denoted by G d . Conf ig-Arr, is an array with the size of m g , whose elements show the partitions each global gate is supposed to be executed. The value of '0' ('1') for the elements of this array means the corresponding gate is assumed to be executed in P 0 (P 1 ). The partition in which the gate g is supposed to be executed based on the Conf ig-Arr array is denoted by g.l. Definition 1 In order to perform a global CNOT gate, one of its two qubits should be teleported from its home partition to another. This qubit is called a migrated qubit, as long as it is not teleported back to its home partition. To keep load balancing of quantum subsystems, it is assumed that at each time, the number of migrated qubits is at most one. For example, in the circuit of Fig. 4, the set G is represented as: {CNOT 1 (0, 0, 1) CNOT 2 (1, 0, 0, 0) CNOT 3 (0, 0, 1, 1) H 4 (1, 1) CNOT 5 (1, 1, 0, 1) H 6 (0, 1) CNOT 7 (0, 1, 1, 1) CNOT 8 (0, 0, 1) CNOT 9 (1, 1, 0, 0)} As non-commutativity property of gates is an important concept in our algorithm, it is considered in the following. First we examine the non-commutativity of two CNOT gates. Two CNOT gates do not commute when the index of control qubit of CNOT gate is the same as the index of target qubit of other gate [33] as shown in Fig. 2. As shown in this figure, the third output in circuit in the left is |b ⊕ c , while it is |a ⊕ b ⊕ c in the circuit in the right. Now the commutativity relations of two adjacent CNOT and a single-qubit gate are considered. 1. If the single-qubit gate, U is applied to the same qubit of control of the CNOT gate, they commute if: where θ ∈ [0, 2π). Examining (1), θ is obtained 0, and U is a diagonal unitary matrix as follows: 2. If the single-qubit gate, U is applied to the target qubit of CNOT gate they commute if that the X gate and U gate commute. X gate and a U gate commute if: Examining (2), we found that θ is either 0 or π. In the case of θ = 0, the structure of U is a unitary matrix as follows: and where θ = π, the structure of U is a unitary matrix as follows: The number of required teleportations for a given DQC, namely its teleportation cost is considered as the figure of merit for the proposed approach as explanted in Section 5.<Proposed Approach>In this section, first the proposed algorithm for optimizing the teleportation cost of a given DQC is explained and then, it is performed on a simple running example.<Conclusion and Future Works>In this study, we presented an algorithm to optimize the number of teleporta-tions for a distributed quantum system consisting of two spatially separated and long-distance quantum subsystems. As teleportation is a costly operation in quantum computation technologies, reducing the number of such operations is very important for designing distributed quantum computers. As future works, proposing a faster algorithm to perform the proposed idea is being considered. Moreover, extending the proposed approach to the case when the number of partitions is more than two can be studied. Finally, the used library of gates can be extended to include three-qubit quantum gates and hence the proposed algorithm should be modified accordingly.

title: Fidelity-Based Ant Colony Algorithm with Q-learning of Quantum System
abstract: Quantum ant colony algorithm (ACA) has potential applications in quantum information processing, such as solutions of traveling salesman problem, zero-one knapsack problem, robot route planning problem, and so on. To shorten the search time of the ACA, we suggest the fidelity-based ant colony algorithm (FACA) for the control of quantum system. Motivated by structure of the Q-learning algorithm, we demonstrate the combination of a FACA with the Q-learning algorithm and suggest the design of a fidelity-based ant colony algorithm with the Q-learning to improve the performance of the FACA in a spin-1/2 quantum system. The numeric simulation results show that the FACA with the Q-learning can efficiently avoid trapping into local optimal policies and increase the speed of convergence process of quantum system.
text: <title>Fidelity-Based Ant Colony Algorithm with Q-learning of Quantum System<abstract>Quantum ant colony algorithm (ACA) has potential applications in quantum information processing, such as solutions of traveling salesman problem, zero-one knapsack problem, robot route planning problem, and so on. To shorten the search time of the ACA, we suggest the fidelity-based ant colony algorithm (FACA) for the control of quantum system. Motivated by structure of the Q-learning algorithm, we demonstrate the combination of a FACA with the Q-learning algorithm and suggest the design of a fidelity-based ant colony algorithm with the Q-learning to improve the performance of the FACA in a spin-1/2 quantum system. The numeric simulation results show that the FACA with the Q-learning can efficiently avoid trapping into local optimal policies and increase the speed of convergence process of quantum system.<Introduction>There are two kinds of control strategies for the optimum designs, i.e., the open-loop control and the closed-loop control. Because there is a simple controller in the open-loop control, which is convenient to be implemented, the open-loop control strategy was initially adopted for solving the optimizing problems in quantum system [1]. It must satisfy the following constraints: i) The system Hamiltonian H 0 is known to high precision. ii) The multidimensional Schr ödinger equation i ∂ψ ∂t = [H 0με(t)]ψ may be reliably solved. iii) The resultant control field design ε(t) may be faithfully reproduced. Unfortunately, it is difficult to practically implement such an open-loop control strategy that satisfies the above-mentioned assumptions, leading to the quantum closed-loop control strategy in the literature [2]. The traditional closed-loop learning control strategy was initially proposed by Rabitz [3]. It is an effective control method for the quantum control, which can optimize the system performance through learning from experience by searching for the best control strategy. It involves three elements, i.e., i) an input initial guess, ii) the laboratory generation of the control applying to the sample and subsequently observed for its impact, and iii) a learning algorithm that considers the prior experiments and suggests the form of the next control input. Designing the appropriate quantum learning control algorithm is an important task for the closed-loop learning control strategy, which includes the gradient algorithm, the genetic algorithm, the linear mapping algorithm, the nonlinear mapping algorithm, the reinforcement learning algorithm, and so on. There is strong robustness required for the gradient algorithm [3], whereas the gradient δJ /δε(t) must be measured with the inherent errors. The genetic algorithm was widely used in quantum control, due to its strong optimization ability and powerful search ability [4]. However a potential difficulty with this algorithm is that it has to work with large numbers of control variables. The input-output relationship of controlled system can be fully considered in the linear mapping algorithm and be simplified to the linear maps. So the linear mapping algorithm can be effectively used in the closed-loop learning control. Because the quantum control systems may be highly nonlinear, the practical application of the linear mapping algorithm has been limited. Under such circumstances, the nonlinear mapping algorithm has been development [5,6]. The integration of the genetic algorithm and the nonlinear algorithm can solve the problem of the chemical quantum system. The reinforcement learning algorithm makes a good tradeoff between exploration and exploitation and hence can speedup the learning rate. However, because of the implementing constraints of the Grover algorithm, the reinforcement learning algorithm can't be used for the practical quantum system. To strengthen the searching speed, the ACA was proposed by Marco Dorigo motivated by the behavior that ants find the optimal path in the feeding process [7]. It is essentially a complex intelligent system. The ACA is a probability algorithm, which simulates the foraging behavior of ants to find an optimal path [8][9][10]. The ACA-based optimality has been deeply studied in the intelligent control and industrial applications [11,12]. However, there exist several issues in developing the ACA-based applications, including tradeoff between exploration and exploitation, search efficiency and search quality [13,14]. After that, the FACA was proposed to solve the above-mentioned problems, only focusing on the transition probability with fidelity-directed exploration strategy in quantum systems [15,16]. Although the FACA can optimize the traditional ACA, the parameter selection process is an intolerable tedious task since it requires a large number of experiments to compare and determine the parameter values. On one hand, the parameter selections of ACA are sensitive and rely on the characteristics of the searching goal. On the other hand, the parameters cannot be transferred from a problem to another. In order to simplify the parameter selection of the ACA and reduce the human interaction with the intelligence, the Q-learning, as a kind of reinforcement learning algorithm, is used for the FACA [17,18], which can fling off environmental restrictions. Through the Q-function training, the agent can determine the optimal strategy by learning in the case of unknown environment models [19,20]. Because the self-learning of the agent replaces the complicated parameter selection process [21], the intellectuality and stability of ACA will be improved. Motivated by unique characteristics of quantum systems that make open loop strategies competitive [22,23], we propose an algorithm to increase the transition probability of the ACA in the complex quantum system [24,25]. For the given set of control fields, we apply the FACA to control laws for solving a class of quantum control problems. In quantum information processing, the closeness between two quantum states can be measured by fidelity [26]. Higher fidelity between the two states represents that their similarity is also higher [27], thus we can use the fidelity to replace the heuristic function between quantum states [28]. The fidelity can be sent back to the transition probability, so we can use it to speedup the solving process to avoid getting lost and getting local optimal solution. Numerical simulations show that the FACA with the Q-learning enables the performance improvement of quantum control systems. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we demonstrate the structure of the ACA. In Section 3, the FACA is designed with the Q-learning in quantum system. In Section 4, we illustrate the applications of the FACA with the Q-learning in the control of a typical class of quantum systems(i.e. spin-1/2 system). In Section 5, we analyze the performance of the proposed algorithm by illustrating the convergence of the FACA with the Q-learning. Finally, conclusion is drawn in Section 6.<Ant Colony Algorithm>To illustrate the mathematical model of ant colony algorithm, the classical combination optimization problem is suggested to determine a shortest path passing through each node one time for n selectable nodes. We assume d ij is the distance between node i and node j , τ ij is the pheromone intensity of path (i, j ), and η ij is the heuristic function, which is the visibility of path and reflects the degree of inspiration from node i to node j . In this section, the value of the heuristic function is given by 1 d ij . The practical ACA can acquire an optimal control strategy of pheromone which is a response to environment or system. At the initial moment, the pheromone of each path is equal to a constant C, i.e., τ ij (0) = C. For the k th ant, it selects the next node according to the amount of pheromone. The transition probability from node i to node j is given by where α is the information heuristic factor that reflects the role of the pheromone accrued by the walking ants, β is the expected heuristic value that represents the effect of the visibility of the heuristic information, and allowed k = {1, 2, • • • , n} represents the possible nodes that the k th ant can select. Different from the real ants, the artificial ant system owns memory function. In order to satisfy the constraint, each ant cannot pass a node twice in one loop, where the table tabu k is designed to record the node that the ant has passed in current time. In this loop the ant is not allowed to go through the node again. In the next loop, the table tabu k is cleared and the ant chooses the next node again. Namely, allowed ktabu k shows the remaining nodes can be selected by the ants in the next step. After repeating the above-mentioned processing n times, and the amount of pheromone for each path is updated according to the constraints (2) where ρ is the persistence coefficient of pheromone, τ ij (t, t + n) is the increment of pheromone on the path (i, j ), τ k ij (t, t + n) is the amount of pheromone left by ant k on the path (i, j ) given by where Q denotes the intensity of pheromone that affects the converging rate of algorithm. The procedure of a classical ant colony algorithm is shown as Algorithm 1. 3 The Improved Ant Colony Algorithm<The Fidelity-based Ant Colony Algorithm>In the traditional ACA, mostly, the reciprocal of the distance between two points is used as the heuristic function. Although the traditional ACA can make the system converge to a certain degree, it needs longer searching time than others and tends to be precocial and stagnant in some station. Thus, if we can extract more information from the system structure or system behavior, the system will converge more easily. Since the concept of fidelity is widely used in quantum and it reflects the internal connection between the input signal and the output signal. Moreover, it could potentially handle the complex quantum problems. Here, we develop a FACA method for control of quantum systems, which can also be applied to some other complex problems and can accelerate the convergence speed of control system. title: Improving Qubit Phase Estimation in Amplitude-damping Channel by Partial-collapse Measurement
abstract: An efficient method is proposed to improve qubit phase estimation in amplitude-damping channel by partial-collapse measurement in this paper. It is shown that the quantum Fisher information (QFI) can be distinctly enhanced under amplitude-damping decoherence with partial-collapse measurement. Moreover, the optimal QFI is approximately close to the maximum value 1 regardless of the decoherence parameter by choosing the appropriate measurement strengths.
text: <title>Improving Qubit Phase Estimation in Amplitude-damping Channel by Partial-collapse Measurement<abstract>An efficient method is proposed to improve qubit phase estimation in amplitudedamping channel by partial-collapse measurement in this paper. It is shown that the quantum Fisher information (QFI) can be distinctly enhanced under amplitude-damping decoherence with partial-collapse measurement. Moreover, the optimal QFI is approximately close to the maximum value 1 regardless of the decoherence parameter by choosing the appropriate measurement strengths.<Introduction>It is well known that the precision of parameter estimation plays a crucial role in quantum metrology. The quantum Cramér-Rao (QCR) inequality [1] gives the best bound of precise parameter estimation, which is associated with quantum Fisher information (QFI) [2]. Consequently, the QFI becomes a key concept in the quantum estimation theory. According to quantum Cramér-Rao inequality, a large QFI means a high precision of parameter estimation. Hence, the enhancement of the QFI has been a very important topic in quantum metrology. Each realistic quantum system inevitably interacts with its environment, which leads to decoherence and considerable decrease of precision of parameter estimation. In recent years, enormous effects have been devoted to how to improve the precision of parameter estimation in the case of open systems. For example, the precision spectroscopy using entangled state in the presence of Markovian dephasing [3] and non-Markovian noise [4] are investigated; The QFI under decoherence channels [5] or in a quantum-critical environment [6] are analyzed; The QFI measured experimentally with photons and atoms are reported [7,8]; It is also reported that the QFI subject to non-Markovian thermal environment [9] could show revival and retardation loss; The parameter-estimation precision in noisy systems could be enhanced by dynamical decoupling pulses [10], redesigned Ramsey-pulse sequence [11] or error correction [12]; Noisy metrology beyond the standard quantum limits is possible when the noise is concentrated along some spatial direction [13]. Other methods, such as quantum feedback [14], quantum screening [15], and non-Markovian environment [16], are also useful to enhance the parameter estimation precision. In this paper, we propose a scheme to improve the precision of qubit phase estimation with the assistance of partial-collapse measurement. Partial-collapse measurement which is also known as weak measurement (note the difference with weak value), is a generalization of von Neumann measurement. By 'partial' or 'weak', we mean that the quantum state doesn t compleltely collapse towards an eigenstate of the measurement operator, and could be reversed with some operations. In some sense, partial-collapse measurement is more valuable than von Neumann measurement, because numerous researches have indeed demonstrated that partial-collapse measurement could be used to steer the quantum state evolution [17,18], protect quantum entanglement and quantum correlations [19][20][21][22][23][24][25]. This motivates us to improve the precision of qubit phase estimation in the presence of noise by utilizing the partial-collapse measurement. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the definitions of quantum Fisher information and partial-collapse measurement and then, in Section 3, theoretical framework of our approach to improve qubit phase estimation in amplitudedamping channel is given. In Section 4, we show how the precision of qubit phase estimation could be enhanced in amplitude-damping channel by partial-collapse measurement. Both analytical and numerical results are given. We offer our conclusions in Section 5.<Quantum Fisher Information and Partial-collapse Measurement>Before describing our scheme, we take some brief reviews of the QFI and partial-collapse measurement approach. In an unknown parameter estimation, the QFI gives a theoretically achievable limit on its precision. According to the quantum Cramér-Rao theorem [1], the mean square fluctuation of φ satisfies the following QCR inequality: where v is the number of independent measurements and F φ is the QFI. The QFI is defined as where ρ(φ) is the density operator of the system, L(φ) is the symmetric logarithmic derivation (SLD), which are Hermitian operators determined by From ( 1), we can see that the large QFI means a high precision of the estimation. Therefore, how to enhance the QFI in quantum metrology becomes an interesting topic. For a single qubit with computational basis |0 and |1 , partial-collapse measurement and measurement reversal can be written, respectively, as a non-unitary quantum operation [26] where m, n ∈ [0, ∞) are the measurement strengths. M is the projective measurement when m = 0. And when m ∈ (0, 1), M is a measurement partially collapsing the quantum system to the ground state. When m ∈ (1, ∞), M partially collapses the quantum system to the excited state. Usually a partial-collapse measurement can be parameterized as M = diag{1, √ 1 -p}, and the measurement reversal operator is written as N = diag{ √ 1p r , 1}. In our article, for convenience and generality, we use M = diag{1, m} and N = diag{n, 1} with m, n ∈ [0, ∞).<Theoretical Framework>We consider an arbitrary single-qubit state |ψ = cos(Q/2)|0 + e iφ sin(Q/2)|1 , where Q [0, π/2] is a measure of entanglement. And, a phase gate U ϕ = |0 0| + e (iϕ) |1 1| is operated on the input state |ψ . So, the output state is given by ρ = U ϕ |ψ ψ|U + ϕ . We can put φ = 0 without loss of generality, thus, the output state is In this paper we address the estimation of ϕ assuming the qubit evolving through a channel affected by amplitude-damping noise. In general, the noisy quantum channels are given in the Kraus representation The operator K l satisfies the CPTP relation l K † l K l = I . In order to improve the QFI, we should perform partial-collapse measurement M and measurement reversal N , before and after the noisy quantum channel, respectively. After these measurements being implemented, the state is, where ε channel is defined by (6). For the sake of simplicity, we introduce a quantity τ = γ t, then s = exp(-τ/2). In the Bloch Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of our approach to improve qubit phase estimation in amplitude-damping channel by partial-collapse measurement. We perform partial-collapse measurement M and measurement reversal N , before and after the noisy channel representation, the ADC squeezes the Bloch sphere into an ellipsoid and shifts it toward the north pole. The radius in the xy plane is reduced by a factor √ s, while in the z direction it is reduced by a factor s. The ADC is a prototype model of a dissipative interaction between a qubit and its environment. Amplitude-damping decoherence is applicable to many practical qubit systems, including vacuum-single-photon qubit with photon loss, atomic qubit with spontaneous decay, and superconducting qubit with zero-temperature energy relaxation. The solid line, dashed line and dashed-dotted line stand for optimal QFI, non optimal QFI with partial-collapse measurement and QFI without partial-collapse measurement, respectively. The results show that the QFI decreases The solid line, dashed line and dashed-dotted line stand for optimal QFI, non optimal QFI with partial-collapse measurement and QFI without partial-collapse measurement, respectively monotonically with time and decays rapidly to zero without partial-collapse measurement. However, the QFI can be improved distinctly with partial-collapse measurement. As measurement strength n increases, the QFI decays more slowly. Moreover, the optimal QFI is always greater than or equal to the non optimal QFI in the dynamic process. According to (17), it is interesting to observe that lim n→∞ F w ϕ (ADCM) = lim n→∞ n 2 s n 2 s+1-s = 1 which means that the optimal QFI approaches a maximum value 1 regardless of the decoherence parameter when measurement strengths n approaches infinity. Note that, The overlap of the solid line and the dashed-dotted line in Fig. 2a is due to the fact that when Q = π/2 and n = 1, we have F ϕ (ADC) = F w ϕ (ADCM) = s according to ( 9) and ( 17). In Figs. 3 and4, we plot the QFI evolution against the parameter τ with Q = π/5 and Q = π/10 respectively. As in the case of Q = π/2, the results show that the QFI can be enhanced greatly with partial-collapse measurement. The QFI decays more slowly with the increase of measurement strength n. Moreover, the optimal QFI is always greater than or equal to the non optimal QFI in the dynamic process. It is interesting to observe that according to (14), lim n→∞ F w ϕ (ADCM) ≈ n 2 s(cos(2Q)-1) 2n 2 s(cos 2 Q-1) = 1 which means that whatever the value of Q, the optimal QFI approaches a maximum value 1 regardless of the decoherence parameter when measurement strengths n approaches infinity.<Conclusion>In this paper, we have proposed a method to improve qubit phase estimation in amplitudedamping channel by partial-collapse measurement. It is shown that the quantum Fisher information can be distinctly enhanced under amplitude-damping decoherence with partialcollapse measurement. Moreover, we have found that the optimal QFI is approximately close to the maximum value 1 regardless of the decoherence parameter by choosing the appropriate measurement strength. Weak measurements have been experimentally realized in various physical systems, e.g., solid systems [27], superconducting phase qubits [28], and linear optic devices [29]. We hope that our proposal can be realized by using such or other systems. Although we have illustrated our protocol for qubit phase estimation in amplitude-damping channel, generalization to parameter estimation with qutrits and parameter estimation in some more general channels seems straightforward. On the other hand, our method could be extended to parameter estimation in noninertial frames. The aspect is of both theoretical and applied significance as the maintenance of quantum Fisher information is a central problem in relativistic quantum metrology [30,31] and relativistic clock synchronization [32,33].

title: Various Quantum Correlations in Two-Qubit Two-Axis Spin Squeezing Model in Thermal Equilibrium under an External Magnetic Field
abstract: This paper investigates the influence of the spin squeezing parameter gamma, the external magnetic field B and the temperature T on the concurrence (C), the quantum discord (QD), and the geometric quantum discord (GQD) in the two-qubit two-axis spin squeezing model in thermal equilibrium under an external magnetic field. The results show that the spin squeezing parameter gamma has a positive effect on all three correlations. When the system is in the ground state, the external magnetic field B has a weakening effect on the three types of quantum correlations. Particularly, the spin squeezing parameter can be used to alleviate the destructive effect of the magnetic field on the geometric quantum discord. At a relatively high temperature, the externally applied magnetic field B helps enhance the quantum discord (QD). Further, the quantum discord is more robust than concurrence, and thus is more suitable for use as a quantum resource in information processing.

The results show that the spin squeezing parameter γ has a positive effect on all three correlations. When the system is in the ground state, the external magnetic field B has a weakening effect on the three types of quantum correlations. Particularly, the spin squeezing parameter can be used to alleviate the destructive effect of the magnetic field on the geometric quantum discord. At a relatively high temperature, the externally applied magnetic field B helps enhance the quantum discord (QD). Further, the quantum discord is more robust than concurrence, and thus is more suitable for use as a quantum resource in information processing.<Introduction>Quantum entanglement has attracted wide attention as an important physical resource for quantum information processing and quantum computation, and has been widely applied to fields like quantum dense coding [1], quantum teleportation [2] and quantum key distribution [3]. However, in actual applications, the entanglement system inevitably interacts with the environment, so that a decoherence effect is generated in quantum computing devices and communication passages, resulting in the attenuation or even sudden disappearance of the entanglement [4][5][6][7][8]. This is a severe obstacle in quantum information processing. Furthermore, quantum entanglement is actually only a specific aspect of quantum correlation, which may not entirely measure all non-classic correlations. In 2001, Ollivier and Zurek [9] proposed a new physical quantity (namely, quantum discord) to measure quantum correlation. However, in the quantum discord calculation [10], the calculation of classic correlation often needs to introduce a set of complete measuring bases, and optimization on all measuring bases is required. Thus, the calculation of quantum discord is often very difficult. To overcome such difficulty, Dakić et al. proposed the concept of geometric quantum discord [11]. As a measurement method of quantum correlation, the geometric quantum discord (GQD) is widely applied to the two-qubit quantum state [12]. Scholars have conducted many studies on quantum correlation of models such as the Heisenberg model [12][13][14], the J -C model [15,16], and the superconducting system [17]; however, the quantum correlation in the spin squeezing model [18][19][20][21] has just started to attracted people's attention in recent years. Furthermore, research regarding the geometric quantum discord of the two-qubit spin squeezing state in thermal equilibrium states has not yet been reported. In this paper, the spin squeezing effect parameter, the temperature and the external magnetic field were controlled to study their impacts on various quantum correlations in the two-qubit two-axis countertwisting model (TACM) in thermal equilibrium states.<Spin Squeezing Model and Density Matrix>The two-axis twisting Hamiltonian corresponds to the simultaneous excitation-deexcitation of two atoms, while the one-axis twisting Hamiltonian corresponds to the energy proportional to the square of the population difference. In spin systems, the squeezing occurs on the phase sphere. Unlike boson squeezing, the quasi probability distribution cannot be homogeneously or globally squeezed in one direction over the whole space. If a spin component is shrunk around a certain point on the sphere, it must be stretched around another point. This imposes a fundamental restriction on the reduction in quantum noise. The two-axis countertwisting mechanism is the one that achieves the maximal noise reduction [22], which is crucial to the quantum information and computing Under the effect of external magnetic effects, the two-qubit spin squeezing model is considered [20], whose Hamiltonian is: where μ and χ represent the spin squeezing effect along the X and Y directions, while γ represents the spin squeezing effect in the XY plane. The collective spin operators are , where σ i α is the i th spin of the Pauli matrix. Here B is the magnetic field strength along the Z-axis [21]. When χ = γ = 0, the Hamiltonian reduces to the one-axis twisting model (OATM). That is: When μ = χ = 0, the Hamiltonian reduces to the two-axis countertwisting model (TACM). That is: When the system is in the thermal equilibrium state, the density matrix may be expressed as: where Z = tr[exp(-βH )] is system partition function, β = 1/kT , k is the Boltzmann constant. For simplicity we work with natural unit system k = 1 henceforth. After calculation, the following density matrix may be obtained: When the model is the TACM model, the eigenvalues E n are as follows: The corresponding eigenstate |ψ n is: and the matrix elements are: where,<Measurement of Quantum Correlation>For a given bipartite quantum state ρ AB , the concurrence between the two qubits is is the Pauli matrix. For a density matrix of the X-type structure, the concurrence (C) of the quantum entanglement has an equivalent expression as follows: where The quantum discord QD(ρ AB ) is defined by the difference in the value between the quantum mutual information I (ρ AB ) and the classic correlation CC(ρ AB ) [9,10], that is where It is not hard to see that the calculation amount of the minimum value in calculation of the quantum discord is very large, and the states that can be resolved are also very limited [10]. Directed towards this difficulty, in 2010, Dakić et al. [10] proposed the concept of geometric quantum discord(GQD): the density matrix ρ of two sub-systems in the Bloch representation may be expressed as: where I represents the identity matrix, σ i (i = x, y, z) is the Pauli matrix, Thus, the corresponding geometric quantum discord is: where a = (a 1 , a 2 , a 3 ) t is the column vector, a 2 = 3 i=1 a 2 i , T = {T ij } is the matrix from (11), T 2 = T r(T t T ), and k max is the maximum eigenvalue of the matrix, aa t + T T t , where the subscript t represents the transposition of the vector or matrix.<Results and Discussion>Using the definitions of the bipartite quantum entanglement, quantum discord and geometric quantum discord, as well as the expression of the density matrix of the two-axis spin squeezing model, we discuss the impacts of different parameters on the thermal entanglement, quantum discord, and the geometric quantum discord of this model. During the analysis, three parameters are used, namely, the spin squeezing effect γ in the XY plane, the magnetic field strength B along the Z axis, and the temperature T First, the influence of different parameters on the concurrence are discussed. Figure 1a andb respectively show the variation of the concurrence when the temperature T changes under different external magnetic fields and spin squeezing parameters γ . Figure 1a and b both show that the concurrence decreases from the maximum value to zero as the temperature T increases. In Fig. 1a, We set the spin squeezing parameter to be γ = 1, and as the external magnetic field increases, the maximum value of the concurrence decreases. In Fig. 1b, where the external magnetic field is 0, as the spin squeezing parameter γ increases the value range of the entanglement broadens, and the attenuation degree decreases. That is, the entanglement robustness is enhanced. Figure 2 illustrates the variation of the quantum discord as the temperature T varies. Figure 2a and b respectively describe the situations under different magnetic fields and spin squeezing parameters γ . As the temperature T increases, in both cases the quantum discord rapidly decreases from the maximum value corresponding to near-zero temperatures (near the ground state) to a value of approximately zero and then gradually revives to a steady-state value. Figure 2a shows that as the external magnetic field grows stronger, though the maximum value of quantum discord decreases, the corresponding attenuation rate decreases, restoration of quantum discord to the steady-state value becomes faster The greater the spin squeezing parameter γ as in Fig. 2b the smaller the attenuation rate of the quantum discord; furthermore, the steady-state value will be eventually reached even though the restoration is comparatively slow. Figure 3 illustrates the variation of the geometric quantum discord with the temperature T . From Fig. 3a andb, as the temperature increases, the geometric quantum discord decreases monotonically, eventually reaching zero. In Fig. 3a, the spin squeezing parameter γ is set to 1 As the external magnetic field increases, the maximum value of the geometric quantum discord reduces significantly. When the external magnetic field B is zero in Fig. 3b, at relatively low temperatures, the geometric quantum discord increases as the spin squeezing parameter γ increases. That is, the spin squeezing parameter γ may, to some extent, counteract the negative effect of the temperature on the geometric quantum discord. In order to describe the interplay between the field and the spin squeezing parameter for the geometric quantum discord, the Fig. 4 is presented. Interestingly, the negative effect of the comparatively stronger magnetic field on the GQD can be alleviated via a larger spin squeezing parameter indicating the possibility of generation of larger GQD in spite of a strong magnetic field. As can be seen from the Fig. 5a, only the quantum discord revives to a steady state value after a sharp decrease starting from the zero temperature, while the other two monotonously decrease to zero as the temperature rises. Figure 5b shows that the spin squeezing parameter in the XY plane plays a positive role for the increasing of all the three correlations.<Conclusion>In summary this paper studied the various correlation measured by concurrence, quantum discord and the geometric quantum discord in the presence of external magnetic field and the spin squeezing parameter in the XY plane of a two-axis countertwisting model (T ACM). The results indicate that the spin squeezing parameter γ plays a constructive role on the three types of correlation, and the external magnetic field B and the temperature T have a weakening effect on the quantum correlation. One exception is that the external magnetic field B is found to have a positive impact on the quantum discord at relatively high temperatures. For the geometric quantum discord, the spin squeezing parameter still can be used to increase it effectively despite the negative effect of magnetic field on it. Last but not the least, the quantum discord is more robust than the geometric quantum discord and the entanglement in a two-qubit two-axis spin squeezing model, thus is more suitable as a quantum resource in information processing.

title: Multi-Hop Teleportation of an Unknown Qubit State Based on W States
abstract: Quantum teleportation is important in quantum communication networks. Considering that quantum state information is also transmitted between two distant nodes, intermediated nodes are employed and two multi-hop teleportation protocols based on W state are proposed. One is hop-by-hop teleportation protocol and the other is the improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation. In hop-by-hop protocol, the transmitted quantum state needs to be recovered at every node on the route. In improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation, intermediate nodes need not to recover the transmitted quantum state. Compared to the hop-by-hop protocol, the improved protocol can reduce the transmission delay and improve the transmission efficiency.
text: <title>Multi-Hop Teleportation of an Unknown Qubit State Based on W States<abstract>Quantum teleportation is important in quantum communication networks. Considering that quantum state information is also transmitted between two distant nodes, intermediated nodes are employed and two multi-hop teleportation protocols based on W state are proposed. One is hop-by-hop teleportation protocol and the other is the improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation. In hopby-hop protocol, the transmitted quantum state needs to be recovered at every node on the route. In improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation, intermediate nodes need not to recover the transmitted quantum state. Compared to the hopby-hop protocol, the improved protocol can reduce the transmission delay and improve the transmission efficiency.<Introduction>In recent years, quantum information has become a hot area in research, and it usually consists of quantum computation and quantum communication [1]. In quantum communication, quantum key distribution [2][3][4][5], quantum secure direct communication [6,7] and quantum teleportation are three major branches which have been widely explored over the past decades. Quantum teleportation is an important transmission protocol in quantum communication and becomes one of the main transmission techniques in quantum networks [8]. Entanglement pairs are the fundamental resource of quantum teleportation [9]. There are many teleportation protocols based on different entangled states, such as Bell state, W state and GHZ state [10][11][12][13][14][15]. Considering that the W states are robust against loss of particles, there have been various teleportation protocols based on W state. For quantum teleportation of single qubit state, Jaewoo Joo et al. proposed a protocol with the constant probability 2/3 using Bellstate measurement and unitary operation [16]. To improve the success probability, Pankaj Agrawal and Arun Pati proposed a method to realize perfect teleportation through a specific set of W states [17]. They found by using von Neumann measurement, a specific class of W states can be teleported with 100% success probability. Usually, only general W state can be generated, researchers are also able to teleport an arbitrary and unknown qubit with Bellstate measurement and complicated unitary transformation [18]. To deliver an unknown two-particle entangled state, Zhuo-Liang Cao and Wei Song proposed a protocol to teleport this kind of state by introducing POVM measurement [19]. How to transfer quantum state effectively in quantum networks is still an open problem. Different from classical network, quantum information can not simply be transmitted and forwarded. And it is unrealistic that a sender shares entanglement resources and classic channels with all the other possible receivers at a long distance [20]. Therefore, how to transmit qubits effectively in a wide quantum communication network needs to be resolved. Multi-hop teleportation protocol provides a way to transmit qubits from source to destination without shared entangled pairs [21,22]. Multi-hop teleportation support high-fidelity, long-distance quantum communication using teleportation-like techniques over shorter distances and forms of error correction ranging from a simple parity check on a Bell pair to extraordinarily complex, full error correction schemes based on the mathematics of topology [23][24][25][26][27][28][29]. However, most discussion of multihop teleportation is based on Bell pair channel [30,31], namely, multi-hop teleportation based on W state channel has not been discussed yet. In this paper, we propose the multi-hop teleportation protocol via W state to implement the transmission in quantum networks. As referred in [16], Alice performs the Bell-state measurement (BM) on the unknown state and her part of a W state. Then Bob measures one of his W-entangled qubit and does specific unitary transformation according to outcome of Alice's Bell-state measurement. So that Bob can recover the unknown state with a certain success probability 2/3. We apply this scheme to multi-hop teleportation. In traditional hop-by-hop protocol, each two neighbor nodes do a complete W states teleportation individually, which means quantum information transferred is recovered in each intermediate node and delay time increases linearly with number of intermediate node. However, in our proposed protocol, each transmitter and receiver share three entangled qubits in W states and all unitary operations are moved to destination node. Therefore, only quantum channels between neighbor nodes and classic routes between each intermediate node and destination node are needed and measurement at each node can be performed parallelly, which leads to implement easily and decreases delay. The probability of success is (2/3) n-1 while n is the number of nodes in a route. Besides, confidentiality can be guaranteed further, beacuse intermediate nodes needn't to recover the transmitted state during teleportation. This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, a quantum network is described. Then, a hop-by-hop teleportation protocol is presented in Section 3. In Section 4, an improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation is proposed. Two<Quantum Network>Figure 1 shows a model of quantum network. There are two kinds of nodes in the model, common quantum communication nodes represented by hollow circles and entanglement distribution nodes represented by filled circles respectively. These nodes are connected by channels called classical channels represented by solid lines and quantum channels represented by dotted lines. The quantum channel between two nodes is composed by the sharing entangled pairs. In quantum domain, common quantum communication nodes are distributed in a large area and they can store quantum qubits and classical information [32][33][34]. Each entanglement distribution node is responsible for generating entangled particles and distributing them within effective quantum distribution range. In other words, entanglement distribution node is able to establish and maintain quantum channels between each two nodes, and the distribution of quantum channels is dynamic while entanglement distribution nodes generate and distribute entangled particles dynamically. Every node in quantum network can work as a quantum router which is responsible for finding and setting up a quantum route. Once quantum route is established [35], one node can communicate with another. In a quantum route shown in Fig. 2, each two adjacent nodes connected by quantum channel are<Hop-by-Hop Teleportation Based on W State>In quantum network, the most direct method of multi-hop teleportation from source node to destination node is teleporting the unknown state hop-by-hop. The one-hop teleportation protocol is shown in Fig. 3. According to Jaewoo Joo's research [16], Alice has a qubit A1 which is going to be sent to Bob. The state of qubit A1 is where |α| 2 + |β| 2 = 1. Alice and Bob share a W state as quantum channel, and the state is First, Alice applies a Bell-state measurement on her qubits A1 and A2. Before measuring, total state of qubits A1, A2, B1 and B2 can be expressed in terms of the Bell basis as follows After Bell-state measurement, the total state is collapsed into one of the four states. Then, Bob measures his qubit B1 under basis |0 and |1 and does specific unitary transformation according to outcome of Alice's Bell-state measurement. Only when the outcome of Bob's measurement is |0 B1 , the original state can be restored at B2. If the outcome is |1 B1 , the teleportation fails. The overall probability of one-hop quantum teleportation is [16] Using one-hop teleportation method to hop-by-hop teleportaton, each intermediate node has to do two measurement and one unitary transformation. To implement valid multihop quantum teleportation, classical and quantum channels must exist between each two intermediate nodes. Figure 4 shows protocol of hop-by-hop teleportation based on W states. In Fig. 1, if node 1 sends a request to teleport a quantum state to node 3, then node 1, 2 and 3 consist a quantum communication route in which each two neighbor nodes shares a classic channel and a quantum channel. Namely, hop-by-hop teleportation protocol can be applied to this case. Considering the probability of each hop, the probability of successful teleportation in a route is where n is the number of nodes in the route.<Improved Multi-Hop Teleportation with Centralized Unitary Transformation>In multi-hop quantum communication network, usually hop-by-hop teleportation protocol is time-consuming proportional to n and the improved multi-hop teleportation with centralized unitary transformation can work in parallelism to improve transmission efficiency. Considering one route containing source node Alice, destination node Bob and intermediate nodes. Alice and Bob are connected indirectly through intermediate nodes in a route. there are quantum channels between neighbors and classical channels between intermediate nodes and destination node. To preform multi-hop teleportation in that case, the improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation is proposed in Fig. 5. In this protocol, the neighbor nodes share three entangled qubits in W states as shown in Fig. 5. For example, qubit A2, C1 and C2 are entangled in W states and Alice owns qubit Fig. 5 Improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation A1 and Candy C1 and C2. Different from hop-by-hop scheme, all unitary operations are moved to destination node. Figure 6 shows the quantum circuit for multi-hop teleportation. To simplify analysis, assumes that there are only three nodes in a route, including source node Alice, intermediate node Candy and destination node Bob. Source node Alice has qubit A1 which is going to be sent to Bob. The state of qubit A1 is where |α| 2 + |β| 2 = 1. Alice and intermediate node Candy share a W state as quantum channel, and the state is First, Alice applies a Bell-state measurement on her qubits A1 and A2 and sends outcome by classical channel to destination node Bob. Before measuring, total state of qubits A1, A2, C1 and C2 can be expressed in terms of the Bell basis as follows Fig. 6 Quantum circuit for multi-hop teleportation After Bell-state measurement, the total state is collapsed into one of the four previous states. The probability of each state is For intermediate node Candy, she measures his qubit C1 under basis |0 and |1 . Only when the Candy's measurement outcome is |0 C1 , the original α and β can be restored. If the outcome is |1 C1 , the teleportation fails. Then, Bell-state measurement is performed on qubits C2 and C3 as Alice does on qubit A1 and A2. Also, Candy needs to send outcome of her Bell-state measurement to Bob. At last, Bob measures his qubit B1 as Candy does on C1. If the outcome is |1 B1 , the teleportation fails. To obtain original state of A1, Bob has to do two specific unitary transformation according to outcomes of Alice and Candy's Bell-state measurement. According to different outcomes, the unitary matrix is shown in Table 2. Assume there is a quantum route with n nodes and quantum information is delivered in sequence. The source node owns qubit 1 1 and 1 2 , destination node owns qubits n 1 and n 2 , and node k owns qubits k 1 , k 2 and k 3 like what figure 2 shows where k is a positive integer from 2 to n -1. Then, in the case of k = 2, suppose f k (|ψ (k-1) 2 ) (k = 2) maps the state of qubit (k -1) 2 to k 2 after Bell-state measurement on qubits (k -1) 2 and (k -1) 3 and successful measurement on qubit k 1 . It is obvious that The quantum circuit for improved multi-hop teleportation is shown in Fig. 6. In order to teleport state of qubit 1 1 , Alice does Bell-state measurement on his qubit 1 1 and 1 2 and sends outcome to Bob through classic channel. Candy and other intermediate nodes measure their first qubit, do Bell-state measurement on second and third qubits and send outcome of Bell-state measurement to Bob through classic channel. Then, Destination hop Bob should measure his only qubit and do specific unitary operations according to received outcome of previous Bell-state measurement. The selection of unitary operators is shown in Table 2. Suppose X i = {0, 1} denotes the state of node i, while i ≥ 2, collapsing to |0 or |1 after measurement on his first qubit. Therefore, the whole teleportation succeeds when X 2 + ... + X n = 0. Assume the state Alice wants to teleport is So, the state of qubit n 2 after whole transmission is Assume U k represents unitary matrix selected through Table 2 according to outcome of node (k -1)'s Bell-state measurement and k is a positive integer from 2 to n. So, we have In the case of successful transmission of all nodes and according to ( 14) to (17), the whole process of transmission can be expressed as As a result, the initial quantum state can be restored and the probability of successful teleportation is In previous proposed scheme of multi-hop teleportation, destination node has to perform n -1 unitary transformation as with hop-by-hop from node 1 to node n. To reduce complexity of the whole communication system, all these n -1 unitary transformation can be converted to one represented by U 2 • • • U n-1 U n because the product of any two unitary matrixes is also unitary so that the number of computation of unitary transformation applied The circuit of improved teleportation protocol is shown in Fig. 7 and U is the new unitary matrix<Comparison Between Two Multi-Hop Teleportation Protocols>In previous section, two multi-hop teleportation protocols are proposed. The comparison between protocols is discussed as follows (Fig. 8). Firstly, improved multi-hop teleportation protocol has more confidentiality. In this protocol, all intermediate nodes needn't to recover the transmitted qubit. However, in hopby-hop protocol or classical communication protocol, each intermediate node can recover transmitted qubit which will weaken the confidentiality. Secondly, improved multi-hop teleportation protocol can reduce delay which is mainly caused by transmission of classical information. Adopting centralized unitary transformation, for each node, the Bell-state measurement can be performed independently and the measurement result is also transmitted to destination independently. Therefore, the nodes except destination can perform these operations in parallelism which will lead to reduce delay caused by hop-by-hop. In packet switched network, delay between two nodes consists of nodal processing delay, queuing delay, transmission delay and propagation delay represented by d proc , d queue , d trans and d prop respectively [36], then the total nodal delay is given by To calculate the accurate delay of two proposed multi-hop teleportation protocols, assumes that the load of classical link is light, so that queuing delay is negligible. Hence, the delay of hop-by-hop teleportation and multi-hop teleportation with centralized unitary transformation are given by ( 21) and ( 22), respectively. It is obvious that delay of multi-hop teleportation with centralized unitary transformation is much more less than the other teleportation protocol especially when the number of intermediate nodes is very large. Finally, the complexity of improved multi-hop teleportation system is reduced. Due to the property of unitary matrix that the product of any two unitary matrixes is also unitary, all unitary transformation which may bring much complexity in destination node can be converted to one.<Conclusion>This paper first introduces a single hop protocol to transmit an unknown qubit using a W state as quantum channel. In this single hop scheme, Alice performs Bell-state measurement and Bob does measurement on one of his particles and performs specific unitary operation on the other particle according to Alice's Bell-state measurement outcome. After that, two multi-hop teleportation protocols are proposed. One is hop-by-hop teleportation and the other is improved multi-hop teleportation with centralized unitary transformation. In hop-by-hop teleportation protocol, every intermediate node needs to recover the quantum state to be transmitted. Therefore, each intermediate node has to do two measurements and one unitary transformation, and classical and quantum channels must exist simultaneously between neighbor nodes. Whereas, in improved protocol with centralized unitary transformation, all unitary operations are moved to the destination node and only classic channels between intermediate and destination nodes are needed. The intermediate nodes needn't to recover the quantum state to be transmitted. Moreover, the improved multi-hop teleportation protocol can be performed in parallelism which reduce delay of communication efficiently. In conclusion, comparing with hop-by-hop teleportation, improved multi-hop teleportation protocol with centralized unitary transformation has better confidentiality, implementability and less delay. Besides, by using both two alternative multi-hop teleportation protocols, quantum routing algorithm can be more efficient and quantum network can be more flexible compared to only one multi-hop teleportation protocol.
