As an illustration, we consider two paradigmatic qubit semigroups: Pauli dynamical maps and phase-covariant dynamics. This result has two interesting implications: it provides a universal constraint for the spectra of qubit Schwarz maps and gives rise to a necessary condition for a Schwarz qubit map to be Markovian.<Introduction>Markovian dynamical semigroups are governed by the celebrated GKLS master equation [1][2][3] ρt = L(ρ t ), with * Author to whom any correspondence should be addressed. Original Content from this work may be used under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. Any further distribution of this work must maintain attribution to the author(s) and the title of the work, journal citation and DOI. where H denotes an effective system Hamiltonian, L k are noise operators, and γ k > 0 are positive transition rates (We set ℏ = 1 and use the standard notations for the commutator and anti-commutator: [A, B] := AB -BA, {A, B} := AB + BA, respectively.) This gives rise to the general representation for the generator of the Markovian semigroup {Λ t = e tL } t⩾0 of completely positive trace-preserving maps (CPTP) [4,5]. Solutions of the GKLS master equation define very good approximations to the evolution of many real systems evolution, provided the system environment interaction is sufficiently weak and there is a large enough separation of timescales for the system and environment [3,[6][7][8]. The requirement for complete positivity gives rise to nontrivial constraints among relaxation rates which characterize the evolution of the system [9][10][11]. They provide information on how fast the system relaxes to an asymptotic state and/or how fast it decoheres, and are expected to serve as an experimental verification of the validity of complete positivity in open quantum dynamics. The spectrum of any GKLS generator is in general complex, however, if ℓ belongs to the spectrum then so does ℓ * . Moreover, there is a leading eigenvalue ℓ 0 = 0 (the corresponding eigenvector corresponds to an invariant state of the evolution), and all remaining eigenvalues satisfy Re ℓ k ⩽ 0. The corresponding relaxation rates are defined by Γ k := -Re ℓ k (for more detailed exposition of spectral properties of maps and generators see e.g. [12][13][14]). It should be stressed that contrary to the rates γ k which depend upon a particular representation of L, the relaxation rates Γ k can be measured in the laboratory. title: Half-blind quantum computation with operation teleportation
abstract: Blind quantum computation enables a client with limited quantum capabilities to delegate a powerful quantum computer for performing confidential quantum computation. This paper identifies a security loophole in the initial universal half-blind quantum computation protocol and resolves it using operation teleportation. Simultaneously, to minimize quantum resource consumption for both the client and the server, the proposed protocol relies on the universal gate set H, T, and CX, and only necessitates the client's ability to prepare qubits in the eigenstates of Pauli gates X and Y or measure qubits based on these gates. Finally, a sample example is provided to illustrate the proposed protocol effectively.
text: <title>Half-blind quantum computation with operation teleportation<abstract>Blind quantum computation enables a client with limited quantum capabilities to delegate a powerful quantum computer for performing confidential quantum computation. This paper identifies a security loophole in the initial universal half-blind quantum computation protocol and resolves it using operation teleportation. Simultaneously, to minimize quantum resource consumption for both the client and the server, the proposed protocol relies on the universal gate set H, T, and CX, and only necessitates the client's ability to prepare qubits in the eigenstates of Pauli gates X and Y or measure qubits based on these gates. Finally, a sample example is provided to illustrate the proposed protocol effectively.<Introduction>When the quantum computer emerges, its control may be limited to a few select organizations and companies, owing to the challenges of maintenance and the substantial resource consumption involved. To enable large-scale quantum computation for the user (client) with limited quantum capabilities or a complete classical computer, the achievement of this goal relies on delegating the computational power of a powerful quantum computer (server). The primary research direction in blind quantum computation (BQC) pertains to the problem of ensuring the confidentiality of algorithms and computation results from the server. The concept of BQC was initially proposed by Childs in 2005 [1]. However, this approach imposes a significant demand for quantum resources from the client. In 2009, Broadbent et al [2] introduced the universal BQC (UBQC) protocol, which is based on the method of measurement-BQC (MBQC) [3][4][5]. Unlike the previous scheme, UBQC only requires the client to possess the quantum capacity to prepare qubits, while simultaneously ensuring that the computational algorithm and results remain concealed from the server. Subsequently, various BQC protocols [6][7][8][9][10][11][12][13] were developed based on this pioneering scheme. Some of these protocols have even been successfully implemented in laboratory experiments. One such approach is the double-server model also proposed in [2], which aims to reduce the quantum consumption of the client and enable a fully classical client in BQC. However, this model prohibits communication between the two servers, making it impractical. In 2014, Li et al [14] declared that an almost classical client under a three-server pattern in BQC exists. Xu and Wang [15] immediately simplified this protocol to a single server pattern. However, Hung and Hwang [16] found a security loophole and demonstrated that an almost classical client cannot resist this quantum attack from the server in these protocols. Subsequently, Morimae et al [17] demonstrated that a complete classical client under a single server pattern in BQC does not exist. Therefore, the optimization of quantum requirement for the client in the single-server model has attracted considerable attention. In this model, Morimae and Fujii [6] proposed that a client who solely performs measurements can achieve BQC by implementing a combination of joint MBQC and the on-signing principle [18]. Subsequently, Li et al [19] further advanced the quantum capabilities at the client side of the UBQC protocol in 2021. Since the target quantum state can be prepared computationally, a client with the ability to perform only logical gates H and T can always prepare the required target state in the UBQC protocol on the state |0⟩ sent by the server. Thus, the client is required to possess one of the three quantum capabilities: preparation, measurement, or execution of single gates, in order to accomplish BQC. It is worth mentioning that the BQC protocol, implemented using the MBQC method, requires a large number of non-input single-qubits in the computational process to protect the algorithm's secrecy from the server. However, in practice, there are cases where the client's algorithm does not require strong confidentiality, such as the Shor and Grover algorithms. Sometimes, the client only aims to obtain a confidential and correct result using a well-known quantum algorithm. In 2017, a protocol called universal half-BQC (UHBQC) was proposed [20]. In this protocol, the server possesses knowledge of the client's algorithm, compromising the blindness of BQC. However, in terms of conserving quantum resources, this protocol significantly reduces the quantum cost for the client compared to the UBQC protocol. The client needs to prepare n × m qubits in UBQC but n qubits in UHBQC, where n and m are the numbers of rows and columns in the brickwork state, respectively. Unfortunately, we have identified a security loophole in the UHBQC protocol, where the server can obtain the actual output state without being detected by the client. To address this loophole, we propose a solution by incorporating the operation teleportation method into BQC, and provide rigorous mathematical proof based on Bayes' formula. This method is suitable for two different types of clients that possess quantum capabilities to prepare or measure a single qubit. The corresponding UHBQC protocol not only reduces the quantum interaction between the client and the server but also minimizes the quantum requirements for them. Specifically, the quantum capability utilized in the proposed protocol for the client is lower than UHBQC and UBQC protocol, i.e. the client could also realize UHBQC with quantum capabilities of preparing qubit in state {|+⟩, |-⟩, | π 2 ⟩, | 3π 2 ⟩} or measuring qubit on the basis of Pauli X and Y. The structure of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the UHBQC protocol's security loophole. Next, we establish a new UHBQC protocol based on operation teleportation to avoid this security problem under different quantum abilities the client possesses in section 3. Then, we give a simple example to demonstrate the proposed protocol clearly in section 4. Finally, we conclude in section 5 and mention possible extensions of this work.<Security loophole>In the UHBQC protocol, the computation result of the client is kept secret from the server, but the algorithm is not. To be specific, the client prepares input qubits with one-time pad encryption (the corresponding definition about one-time pad can be seen in [2,[20][21][22]), which likes X i Z j |ψ⟩ for each qubit in form. The server performs quantum computation on these encrypted qubits by applying the universal set of gates {H, S, CX, Toffli} according to the client's instructions. At this stage, the server can directly implement the gates H, S, and CX since they are Clifford gates (the corresponding definition about Clifford gate can be seen in equation (96) of [22]). However, when the client wants to perform a Toffli gate, the server needs to implement additional Clifford gates CZ, CX, and SWAP based on the one-time pad encryptions of the three qubits involved in this gate. This is necessary to mitigate the impact of exchanging the encryption operators X j Z k , X l Z m , X o Z p with the non-Clifford gate Toffli. To ensure the confidentiality of the one-time pad encryptions provided by the server, Tan et al propose a method where the server returns three qubits to the client. The client applies additional Pauli gates (X a and Z b ) to the returned qubits while keeping the values of a and b secret from the server. The client then transfers these three qubits to the server with updating the one-time pad encryption. They declare that the updated one-time pad encryption remains secret from the server. However, there is a security loophole in the above process. Before performing the Toffli gate, the server can transfer half of the particles from each of the three pairs of Bell states to the client, so that he can easily obtain the updated one-time pad encryption by measuring these particles in the Bell basis. Then, she delegates Bob to perform a gate Toffoli in these three qubits. Then, Bob returns them to Alice. During the computation process, the values of θ in A2 and δ in C3 are restricted to the set {0, π 2 , π, 3π 2 }. As a result, steps A1-A3 and C1-C4 can be completed by a client possessing the mentioned quantum abilities. During the input preparation process, as any state can be prepared through computation in the diagram, the client only needs to prepare certain inputs with a one-time pad. In protocol 1, the state of the input could be X ⟩; in protocol 2, Alice only needs to measure the qubit in the X and Y bases to prepare the input using a one-time pad in step B2. To clearly demonstrate our protocol, we provide a simple example below. Let's suppose Alice wants to implement the Grover search algorithm for the target state |00⟩. The corresponding IBM Quantum circuit diagram can be seen in figure 3. At first, Alice random prepares two qubits in state X a1 Z b1 | π 2 ⟩ 1 and X a2 Z b2 |+⟩ 2 . Second, Alice transmits the diagram to Bob as figure 4, based on the state of the input and some relationships X = HZH, Z = T 4 , S = T 2 and H 2 = I. Then, Bob implemented each gate as in this diagram. When the gate is T, Bob performs it as steps A1-A3 or C1-C4 with Alice according to her quantum ability. When the gate is H or CX, Bob performs it directly. Finally, Bob returns all output to Alice successively.<Conclusion>Except for addressing the security loophole in the initial UHBQC protocol, it is also meaningful to compare the quantum capability requirements of our protocol with it. In the [20], the server is expected to perform gates H, S, CX, Toffoli, whereas in our protocol, the server only needs to perform gates H, T, CX and prepare auxiliary qubits. This approach avoids situations where the server has simultaneous control over three qubits and eliminates the need for implementing additional gates like CX, CZ, SWAP to achieve a correct Toffoli gate. In essence, our protocol reduces the quantum resources required by the server, resulting in a decrease in commission costs paid by the client. Furthermore, in their scheme, the client needs two quantum interactions (receiving corresponding qubits and transmitting them) to realize a non-Clifford gate. In contrast, our protocol simplifies this to a single interaction, where the client only transmits or receives qubits. Moreover, our UHBQC protocol can be implemented by a client who is limited to preparing qubits in states |+⟩, |-⟩, | π 2 ⟩, | 3π 2 ⟩ (rather than arbitrary quantum states) or measuring qubits in the X and Y bases. Thus, the quantum abilities required from the client are lower compared to the UBQC protocol, and further UHBQC protocol. In 2018, Liu et al also pointed out that these is a security loophole in the UHBQC protocol. They repaired it by the manner that the client transmits a multi-particle fixed sequence, and the server implements a multi-operation fixed sequence in each round. However, the client in this protocol needs a quantum capability of implementing two-particle operation SWAP. This enhances the difficulty of realizing HBQC for client. In our protocol, the client only needs to prepare single-qubit or measure single-qubit, which is more convenient and easy to realize. In summary, we have developed a novel UHBQC protocol that reduces the quantum resource consumption for both the client and the server. The protocol can also be easily extended to accommodate different quantum capabilities for the client, such as performing only gate operations. Finally, the advantage of HBQC is obviously in terms of the number of qubits that client transmits compared with BQC. However, its disadvantage of it is also obviously, i.e. , the delegated algorithm of the client is not secrecy from the server. Therefore, it is meaningful to develop a BQC protocol with less transmitted qubits as HBQC in the future.

title: Moments based entanglement criteria and measures
abstract: Quantum entanglement plays a key role in quantum computation and quantum information processing. It is of great significance to find efficient and experimentally friend separability criteria to detect entanglement. In this paper, we firstly propose two easily used entanglement criteria based on matrix moments. The first entanglement criterion only uses the first two realignment moments of a density matrix. The second entanglement criterion is based on the moments related to the partially transposed matrix. By detailed examples we illustrate the effectiveness of these criteria in detecting entanglement. Moreover, we provide an experimentally measurable lower bound of concurrence based on these moments. Finally, we present both bipartite and genuine tripartite entanglement measures based on the moments of the reduced states. By detailed examples, we show that our entanglement measures characterize the quantum entanglement in a more fine ways than the existing measures.
text: <title>Moments based entanglement criteria and measures<abstract>Quantum entanglement plays a key role in quantum computation and quantum information processing. It is of great significance to find efficient and experimentally friend separability criteria to detect entanglement. In this paper, we firstly propose two easily used entanglement criteria based on matrix moments. The first entanglement criterion only uses the first two realignment moments of a density matrix. The second entanglement criterion is based on the moments related to the partially transposed matrix. By detailed examples we illustrate the effectiveness of these criteria in detecting entanglement. Moreover, we provide an experimentally measurable lower bound of concurrence based on these moments. Finally, we present both bipartite and genuine tripartite entanglement measures based on the moments of the reduced states. By detailed examples, we show that our entanglement measures characterize the quantum entanglement in a more fine ways than the existing measures.<Introduction>Quantum entanglement [1] is a novel characteristic of quantum mechanics and plays an important role in many quantum tasks such as quantum communications [2][3][4][5], quantum simulation [6], quantum computing [7][8][9] and quantum cryptography [10][11][12]. In this context, detecting the quantum entanglement has become particularly important. Let H A and H B denote the Hilbert spaces of systems A and B with dimensions m and n, respectively. A quantum state ρ ∈ H A ⊗ H B is separable if it can be expressed as a convex combination of product states, Otherwise, the state ρ is entangled. Generally it is a challenge to detect the entanglement for a given state. The PPT criterion [13] is both necessary and sufficient for the separability of quantum states in systems 2 ⊗ 2 and 2 ⊗ 3 [14]. This criterion indicates that for any bipartite separable state ρ, the matrix ρ τ obtained from partial transpose with respect to subsystem B is still positive semi-definite, where (ρ τ ) ij,kl = (ρ) il,kj . Any state that violates the PPT criterion is an entangled one. The realignment is another permutation of the elements of a density matrix. The realignment criterion [15,16] says that for any bipartite separable state ρ, the trace norm of the realigned matrix ρ R is not greater than 1, i.e. ∥ρ R ∥ ⩽ 1, where (ρ R ) ij,kl = (ρ) ik,jl , and the trace norm of an operator E is defined by ∥E∥ := Tr( √ E † E). A state is entangled if it violates the realignment criterion. There are also many other approaches to detect the entanglement. The entanglement witnesses can be used to detect the entanglement [17][18][19] experimentally, although the construction of the witness operators generally requires the prior deterministic information of the quantum state. Locally randomized measurements [20][21][22][23][24] and parameterized entanglement monotone [25][26][27][28][29] have been also adopted to detect entanglement. Besides, the quantum entanglement is also studied based on the truncated moment problem that is well studied mathematically. Bohnet et al proposed a necessary and sufficient condition of separability that can be applied by using a hierarchy of semi-definite programs [30]. Recently, the authors in [31,32] show that the first three partially transpose (PT) moments can be used to detect entanglement. The advantage of the PT moments is that they can be experimentally measured through global random unitary matrices [33,34] or local randomized measurements [31] based on quantum shadow estimation [35]. In [32] the authors proposed a separability criterion based on PT moments called p 3 -OPPT criterion. Neven et al proposed an ordered set of experimentally measured conditions for detecting entanglement [36], with the kth condition given by comparing the moments of the PT density operator up to order k. Zhang et al introduced a separability criterion based on the rearrangement moments [37]. In [38] the authors introduced Λ-moments with respect to any positive maps Λ. They showed that these Λ-moments can effectively characterize the entanglement of unknown quantum states without prior reconstructions. In [39], the authors proposed a framework for designing multipartite entanglement criteria based on permutation moments. The author in [40] demonstrates that for two-qubit quantum systems the PT moments can be expressed as functions of principal minors and shows that the PT moments can detect all the negative partial transpose entanglement of GHZ and W states mixed with white noise. A separability criterion and its physical realization has been also proposed by using the moments of the realigned density matrices [41,42]. Besides the separability, the quantification of entanglement is also of great significance [43]. Some entanglement measures have been proposed to quantify the entanglement [18,19,[44][45][46][47], among which one of the most well known measures is the concurrence [18,19,44]. Let |ψ AB ⟩ be a bipartite pure state in where ρ A = Tr B (|ψ AB ⟩⟨ψ AB |) is the reduced density matrix. The concurrence for general bipartite mixed states ρ is given by the convex-roof extension, where p i ⩾ 0, ∑ i p i = 1 and the minimum is taking over all possible pure state decompositions of ρ = ∑ i p i |ψ i ⟩ AB ⟨ψ i |. For multipartite systems, the quantification of the genuine multipartite entanglement remains a challenging problem. The authors in [48] proposed a genuine multipartite entanglement measure (GMEM) based on the concurrences under bi-partitions. The authors in [49] introduced a genuine three-qubit entanglement measure in terms of the area of a triangle with the three edges given by bipartite concurrences. More genuine multipartite entanglement measures have been also presented [50][51][52][53]. In [51] the authors proposed the generalized geometric measure. Further genuine multipartite concurrences are studied in [53]. Guo et al [54] gave an approach of constituting genuine m-partite entanglement measures from any bipartite entanglement and any k-partite entanglement measure for 3 ⩽ k < m. Recently, the authors in [55] constructed a proper genuine multipartite entanglement measure by using the geometric mean area of concurrence triangles according to a series of inequalities related to entanglement distribution. In this paper, we first propose two separability criteria based on moments, and illustrate their effectiveness in entanglement detection by specific examples. We then provide an experimentally measurable lower bound of concurrence based on the moments. We present a bipartite entanglement measure based on the moments of the reduced states. Furthermore, we propose a genuine tripartite entanglement measure based on our bipartite entanglement measure. The paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we provide a separability criterion based on realignment moments. In section 3, we propose a separability criterion based on PT moments. In section 4, we derive an experimentally measurable lower bound of concurrence for arbitrary bipartite states. In section 5, we propose a bipartite entanglement measure based on reduced moments. In section 6, we put forward a genuine tripartite entanglement measure based on our bipartite entanglement measure. title: Full network nonlocality sharing in extended bilocal scenario via weak measurements with the optimal pointer
abstract: The investigation of network nonlocality (NN) has expanded the study of quantum nonlocality, yet it fails to fully capture the complexities within quantum networks. Recently, a stronger and more genuine definition of NN, known as full quantum network nonlocality (FNN), has been explored, which is considered a vital resource for realizing network-based device-independent quantum cryptography protocols. In this work, we explore the recycling of FNN as quantum resources by analyzing the FNN sharing between different combinations of observers. The FNN sharing in an extended bilocal scenario (consisting of two independent two-qubit quantum states as sources) via weak measurements has been thoroughly discussed. Based on the different motivations of the observer-Charlie1, two types of possible FNN sharing, passive FNN sharing and active FNN sharing, can be investigated by checking the simultaneous violation of Kerstjens-Gisin-Tavakoli inequalities between Alice-Bob-Charlie1 and Alice-Bob-Charlie2. Our results show that passive FNN sharing is impossible while active FNN sharing can be achieved through proper measurements, indicating that FNN sharing in this scenario requires more cooperation by intermediate observers compared to Bell nonlocality sharing and NN sharing.
text: <title>Full network nonlocality sharing in extended bilocal scenario via weak measurements with the optimal pointer<abstract>The investigation of network nonlocality (NN) has expanded the study of quantum nonlocality, yet it fails to fully capture the complexities within quantum networks. Recently, a stronger and more genuine definition of NN, known as full quantum network nonlocality (FNN), has been explored, which is considered a vital resource for realizing network-based device-independent quantum cryptography protocols. In this work, we explore the recycling of FNN as quantum resources by analyzing the FNN sharing between different combinations of observers. The FNN sharing in an extended bilocal scenario (consisting of two independent two-qubit quantum states as sources) via weak measurements has been thoroughly discussed. Based on the different motivations of the observer-Charlie 1 , two types of possible FNN sharing, passive FNN sharing and active FNN sharing, can be investigated by checking the simultaneous violation of Kerstjens-Gisin-Tavakoli inequalities between Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 and Alice-Bob-Charlie 2 . Our results show that passive FNN sharing is impossible while active FNN sharing can be achieved through proper measurements, indicating that FNN sharing in this scenario requires more cooperation by intermediate observers compared to Bell nonlocality sharing and NN sharing.<Introduction>With the increasing demand for increasingly complex quantum networks in numerous quantum information tasks, a deep understanding of quantum correlations within networks has become crucial [1]. Recently, a series of studies on network nonlocality (NN) that may transcend Bell nonlocality, have been reported [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]. The bilocal scenario [2,[4][5][6], which corresponds to the scenario underlying entanglement-swapping experiments [10][11][12], is the simplest quantum network scenario, in which two independent sources share entangled pairs with three observers. Saunders et al [8] demonstrated that NN can be exhibited by violating a network Bell inequality, Branciard-Rosset-Gisin-Pironio (BRGP) inequality, revealing the incompatibility between quantum systems and the BLHV model. However, violating inequalities associated with the BLHV model does not accurately capture all the complexities of nonlocality in entanglement-swapping networks [13]. For instance, in a quantum network where only one source is entangled, regardless of whether remaining parts are correlated or not, the BRGP inequalities from [4] can be always violated [8]. This is evidently a rather trivial form of network correlation, lacking any new valuable physical implications. Excluding network structures that mimic standard Bell nonlocality forms remains a central and highly challenging issue in this field [1,13,14]. In 2022, Pozas-Kerstjens et al [13] elucidated the concept of full network nonlocality (FNN), describing the correlation where all links in the network must share nonlocality resources. FNN implies that there exist correlation properties in the network that cannot be simulated by local variable sources anywhere in the network. Quantum networks with FNN can never be described by models where at least one source satisfies a local hidden variable interpretation while others exhibit generalized nonlocal correlations [13]. It is only constrained by the condition of no-signaling, which implies that even with the existence of new physical systems surpassing quantum correlations, FNN does not permit the possibility of the aforementioned model. Therefore, as a stronger form of NN achievable based on quantum theory, FNN is sufficient to ensure the implementation of network-based device-independent quantum cryptographic protocols. It is more feasible than the groundbreaking work on quantum communication network security protocols [15], which requires systems with distributions stronger than quantum from all sources to limit the information accessible to eavesdroppers. Additionally, FNN has been proven as a crucial resource for quantum random number generation [1,16]. Nevertheless, further investigation is still limited by the little knowledge of FNN and the lack of research tools. The successful methodologies of exploring the standard Bell nonlocality can be adapted to explore FNN. For instance, the investigations of the recycling nonlocality via sequential measurements have provided a special perspective for deeply understanding traditional quantum correlations. The pioneering work of this type of research originated from 2015, Silva et al [17] demonstrated that Bell nonlocality can be shared among more than two observers using weak measurements. Since then, a series of investigations of nonlocal sharing has been reported both in theories [17][18][19][20][21][22][23][24][25] and experiments [26][27][28][29][30][31]. The previous investigations indicate that traditional Bell nonlocality sharing, based on the motivation of intermediate observers, can be divided into active nonlocal sharing and passive nonlocal sharing [20], and has been experimentally verified [28]. Recently, Hou et al [32] studied network nonlocal sharing based on weak measurements in extended bilocal scenarios, where active and passive network nonlocal sharing also exist. Inspired by these studies, we aim to understand whether FNN sharing also exhibits such classification and whether there are differences between NN sharing and FNN sharing. Undoubtedly, it is a particularly interesting prospect to study the difference between the sharing (recycling) of NN and FNN, which not only benefits deeply understanding of FNN, but also provides new insight into quantum tasks in networks, such as network random number generation and network quantum cryptography, etc. In this paper, we investigate the phenomenon of FNN sharing in the extended bilocal scenario as illustrated in figure 1, and delve into two possible types of FNN sharing according to multiple violations of Kerstjens-Gisin-Tavakoli (KGT) inequalities, where they are distinguished based on the different motivations of the intermediate observer Charlie 1 . Whether Charlie 1 is willing to share FNN with Charlie 2 corresponds to either passive sharing or active sharing. Passive sharing means that Charlie 1 does not consciously share FNN with Charlie 2 , but just wants to maximally exhibit the FNN of Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 . In this case, Charlie 1 always chooses the optimal measurement operators to obtain the maximal violations of the KGT inequalities for Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 , which is only limited by the precision factor G. So passive FNN sharing can be exhibited by maximizing the violation of KGT inequalities for Alice-Bob-Charlie 2 , subject to the maximization of the violation of KGT inequalities for Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 . However, active sharing implies that Charlie 1 is aiming to assist Charlie 2 in observing the FNN for Alice-Bob-Charlie 2 , under the constraint that the FNN for Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 can be demonstrated. In this case, Charlie 1 will adjust measurement choices to maximize the simultaneous violation of KGT inequalities for both Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 and Alice-Bob-Charlie 2 , ensuring that the two violation values are the same. To better analyze the two types of FNN sharing, we first demonstrated the maximal violation of KGT inequalities in a bilocal scenario, which can achieve √ 13 ≈ 3.6055 when Alice and Charlie 1 chose the proper measurements. Subsequently, we analyze whether passive FNN sharing and active FNN sharing can be achieved by investigating the simultaneous violation of KGT inequalities between Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 and Alice-Bob-Charlie 2 in the extended bilocal scenario using proper weak measurements with the optimal pointer [17]. Conversely, active FNN sharing can be observed, as the simultaneous violation of KGT inequalities between Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 and Alice-Bob-Charlie 2 exists. Subsequently, in section 3, we tightly demonstrated the maximal violation of KGT inequalities in a bilocal scenario. Passive FNN sharing and active FNN sharing are completely analyzed in section 4. The noise resistance of active FNN sharing is discussed. Initially, we exhibited the optimal FNN by the maximal violation of KGT inequality of Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 , when the scenario regresses to the standard bilocal. It is shown that the maximal violation of KGT inequality can achieve √ 13 ≈ 3.6055 when , which is larger than the previous result 5 √ 2 ≈ 3.5355 [13] with The greater the violation reaches, the easier the experiment carries out. Furthermore, the recycling of FNN as quantum resources by analyzing the FNN sharing between different combinations of observers in the extended bilocal scenario has been explored. According to the different motivations of Charlie 1 in their measurement process, we have completely discussed the possibility of two typical FNN sharing, passive FNN sharing and active FNN sharing respectively. Our results clearly demonstrated that the passive FNN sharing is impossible, as the maximal simultaneous achievement of KGT values R 1 and R 2 for Alice-Bob-Charlie 1 and Alice-Bob-Charlie 2 is 2.9596, which means that the KGT inequalities cannot be simultaneously violated by these different combinations of observers Alice-Bob-Charlie m . These results indicate that, compared with Bell nonlocal sharing and network nonlocal sharing, FNN sharing requires more cooperation by the intermediate observers [20,32]. Additionally, this finding offers fresh insights into applying quantum correlation sharing in quantum cryptography. As passive FNN sharing does not exist, it cannot achieve network-based device-independent quantum cryptographic protocols for the assembly of different multiple observers. Conversely, active FNN sharing ensures the feasibility of this application. This conclusion offers fresh insights into applying FNN sharing in quantum cryptography. Moreover, we also discussed the noise immunity of FNN or active FNN sharing in this scenario. Discussion-FNN is a stronger network correlation form than NN in quantum networks [13]. Our research shows that FNN is more difficult to share than NN in the extended bilocal scenario [32] when the two independent sources are qubit systems. This feature is similar to that in standard quantum correlation sharing, where the sharing of quantum steering is easier to achieve than Bell nonlocality sharing [22,24]. The notion of FNN has just been defined, and the acknowledgment of it is very limited. It will be helpful to depict the FNN from different perspectives [1,13]. The identification criteria of FNN are still very limited, except for KGT inequality. Until now, the scope of FNN witnessed by KGT inequality is unknown. An efficient witness for determining FNN is required. The difficulty of FNN sharing may also be due to the lack of efficient witnesses. Our results will also stimulate the development of deeply investigating these methods of characterizing FNN, and maybe provide a new improvement for quantum tasks in networks.

title: Complex quantum networks: a topical review
abstract: These are exciting times for quantum physics as new quantum technologies are expected to soon transform computing at an unprecedented level. Simultaneously network science is flourishing proving an ideal mathematical and computational framework to capture the complexity of large interacting systems. Here we provide a comprehensive and timely review of the rising field of complex quantum networks. On one side, this subject is key to harness the potential of complex networks in order to provide design principles to boost and enhance quantum algorithms and quantum technologies. On the other side this subject can provide a new generation of quantum algorithms to infer significant complex network properties. The field features fundamental research questions as diverse as designing networks to shape Hamiltonians and their corresponding phase diagram, taming the complexity of many-body quantum systems with network theory, revealing how quantum physics and quantum algorithms can predict novel network properties and phase transitions, and studying the interplay between architecture, topology and performance in quantum communication networks. Our review covers all of these multifaceted aspects in a self-contained presentation aimed both at network-curious quantum physicists and at quantum-curious network theorists. We provide a framework that unifies the field of quantum complex networks along four main research lines: network-generalized, quantum-applied, quantum-generalized and quantum-enhanced. Finally we draw attention to the connections between these research lines, which can lead to new opportunities and new discoveries at the interface between quantum physics and network science.
text: <title>Complex quantum networks: a topical review<abstract>These are exciting times for quantum physics as new quantum technologies are expected to soon transform computing at an unprecedented level. Simultaneously network science is flourishing proving an ideal mathematical and computational framework to capture the complexity of large interacting systems. Here we provide a comprehensive and timely review of the rising field of complex quantum networks. On one side, this subject is key to harness the potential of complex networks in order to provide design principles to boost and enhance quantum algorithms and quantum technologies. On the other side this subject can provide a new generation of quantum algorithms to infer significant complex network properties. The field features fundamental research questions as diverse as designing networks to shape Hamiltonians and their corresponding phase diagram, taming the complexity of many-body quantum systems with network theory, revealing how quantum physics and quantum algorithms can predict novel network properties and phase transitions, and studying the interplay between architecture, topology and performance in quantum communication networks. Our review covers all of these multifaceted aspects in a self-contained presentation aimed both at network-curious quantum physicists and at quantum-curious network theorists. We provide<Introduction and motivation>Quantum physics emerged in the 20th century to explain phenomena not accounted for by classical physics, such as the spectrum of black body radiation and the photoelectric effect, and has since been developed into a mature and highly successful theory of Nature. Its deviations from its classical counterpart have more recently been recognized as an opportunity especially in computing [1], sensing [2], communication [3] and simulation [4]. In this context, regimes or circumstances have been identified where quantumness can provide an advantage or indeed, facilitate an otherwise impossible task. Discovery and pursuit of these new applications has led to the creation of several specialized subfields such as quantum enhanced approaches to classical tasks or generalizing purely classical concepts to the quantum case, further fueling both theoretical and experimental progress towards realizing the envisioned technology. Today we already enjoy the fruits of the so called first quantum revolution which gave us the transistor, the laser and the atomic clock. The second revolution is generally considered to mean that deeply quantum phenomena such as entanglement move from laboratories to the field and their applications are commercialized, meaning in particular that one has to deal with states, systems and architecture of increasing complexity-among the many formidable hurdles to be overcome, this complexity must be tamed [5,6]. While physics in the past centuries has followed mostly a reductionist direction, in this last century we have witnesses the recognition that 'more is different' [7], i.e. new physics arises from large complex interacting systems. In particular starting from the late nineties, complexity has flourished thanks to the increased understanding of complex interacting systems in terms of their underlying network structure [8,9]. Network theory [10,11] is now pivotal to characterize complexity across domains, ranging from the Internet to the brain [12]. Specifically, a complex system is formed by a set of interacting elements, where typically these interactions are considered pairwise. Examples of networks representing complex systems are We distinguish between four distinct research lines on complex quantum networks: network-generalized, quantum-applied, quantum-generalized and quantumenhanced. Here these research lines are schematically presented with a figure and with illustrative research questions. These different research lines will be presented in the indicated sections. not only communication, transportation networks, and power grids, but also protein-protein interaction networks in the cell and neural networks in the brain. More in general networks can be considered as representation of both classical and quantum data. For example networks can be used as a mathematical representation of quantum statistics [13] or they can capture the complexity of entangled spin chains [14,15]. Networks encode the information of complex systems in their topology, hence a fundamental goal of network science has been to mine network structures finding the key statistical and topological properties. Interestingly while some properties are very specific of some complex systems other properties such as the small world [8] property and the scale-free [9] degree distribution, are ubiquitous and define universality classes. A key result of network science is that the topology of the network strongly affects dynamical processes defined on these structures [16]. For instance scale-free networks as different as the Internet or the biological transcription networks respond to random and targeted damage [16][17][18] of their nodes in a similar way, which is very distinct from the response of lattices and random graphs to similar perturbations. This review focuses on the intersection between quantum physics and network theory and therefore on cases where there is both a quantum and a network aspect. Although such research has seen steadily increasing interest since 2000s, the term complex quantum network still does not have a stringent definition and the various research lines have developed independently. However the field is now developing further and we strongly believe that with the impressive advances in the pursuit of quantum technology it is now very timely to cover these multifaceted complex quantum networks and introduce the emerging field in a pedagogical, selfcontained and comprehensive review. This topical review is intended both for quantum physicists and network scientists to serve as an entry point to the literature, complementing and in some ways extending the treatment of previous reviews [5,6]. We distinguish between four main directions of investigation of complex quantum networks. In a similar vein to Dunjko's and Wittek's categorization [19] of quantum machine learning [20][21][22], we call these different research lines quantum-applied, network-generalized, quantum-generalized and quantum-enhanced approaches, respectively. We summarize them in figure 1. Quantum physics research generalizing to or taking inspiration from networks (the network-generalized research line) includes optimizing excitation transport in networks [23] or studying synchronization in open networks of interacting quantum harmonic oscillators [24]. In general, in this line of research the network structure is typically encoded into the system Hamiltonian. Thus important developments have considered quantum critical phenomena [25] on lattices, graphs and complex networks and quantum walks [26,27]. This latter are playing an important role for quantum computation [1] providing significant speedups of quantum algorithm with respect to classical algorithms [28,29] in some network topology. Moreover, research investigating network nonlocality in terms of Bell inequalities [30] or quantum steering [31] also follows in this research line. The quantum-applied research direction includes adopting a network approach to address a quantum problem, such as predicting a quantum phase transition [32] or discovering a previously unknown collective phenomenon [33] from a judiciously chosen network representation of the considered state. The very active quantum generalized research direction identifies quantum concepts that are useful for modelling and characterizing complex networks. This line of research includes the formulation of the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) [13] in complex networks, the definition the von Neumann entropy [34] and of the topological Dirac operator [35] of a network. Finally, the quantum-enhanced research line includes quantum enhanced communication such as quantum key distribution [36] or entanglement distribution [37] and its various applications. The review is structured as follows. The basics of quantum theory and network theory are covered in sections 2 and 3, respectively. They provide a relatively broad selection of topics to account for the variety of ways they can and have been combined with a special emphasis on content relevant to reviewed material, and are intended primarily for readers unfamiliar with either field. The following Sections each focus on a different aspect of complex quantum networks. They are mostly independent and may be read in any order or individually as per interest-for the sake of compactness, the related examples primarily highlight some relevant contemporary research, while technical details are often left for more specialized reviews which are suggested where necessary. Section 4 focuses on network-generalized research and specifically on cases where the network is embedded in the Hamiltonian, often such that the interaction terms play the role of links and the systems the role of nodes. The following section 5 focuses on quantum-applied research where a judicious network representation is sought to simplify, predict, understand or discover properties of interest. Network theory oriented research is covered from two complementary points of view with network models exhibiting emergent quantumness presented in section 6 and quantum algorithms for both conventional and novel properties of classical networks given in section 7. Section 8 focuses on quantum-enhanced communication networks including quantum key distribution and entanglement distribution networks but also briefly introduces state transfer in networks interacting quantum systems as well as network generalized nonlocality. Finally, conclusions are drawn in section 9 where we discuss the overall state of the field and outlook, as well as the connections between the research lines, which we hope encourages cross-fertilization and fosters new research in this promising field.<Basics of quantum mechanics>nan<Basics of network theory>nan<Quantum dynamics in networks>nan<Network representation of quantum systems>nan<Emergence in network models>nan<Quantum algorithms for network inference>nan<Quantum communication networks>nan<Discussion and future directions>Whereas complexity is what empirical networks seem to naturally gravitate towards, quantumness is coy and needs to be cajoled to manifest by isolation of the systems. The two meet in the following research lines: network-generalized quantum problems, quantum-applied network theory, quantum-generalized approaches for complex networks and quantum-enhanced communications, which are currently pursued by scientists and researchers from a variety of backgrounds. In this review we have introduced the four main research lines, unified them under the broader context of complex quantum networks and provided a comprehensive overview of the field. There are multiple promising directions for further development of the field. From the quantum systems perspective, new ways to generalize quantum phenomena to a network scenario can be envisioned. We highlight chiral quantum walks as an example where the underlying graph is no longer undirected and which can have advantages over both classical and sometimes also conventional quantum walks [219][220][221]. Regarding quantum correlations in a network scenario, most work still focuses on Bell nonlocality, leaving room for other types: steering [31], entanglement and discord. Speaking of applications of network theory to the quantum case, a network description of a stationary state has already been explored as a cheaper alternative to state tomography [14,32,248,249] but generalization to evolving states and process tomography has only been suggested. Using a network description to not only detect but to discover previously unknown phenomena [33,250] remains in its infancy. Pivoting to quantum enhanced communication networks, both within reach trusted node and ideal quantum repeater networks can be modeled compactly as just a network of channels weighted by capacities. This description can be applied without a deep understanding of the relevant physics and the results have a clear interpretation. Introducing similar models for the NISQ stage covering the large gap between near term and nearly ideal is undoubtedly challenging but if it could be done the field could have contributions from researchers from a much wider variety of backgrounds and specializations. From the network science perspective the field of complex quantum networks could also be transformative. For instance the new generation of quantum computers could lead to the flourishing of quantum algorithms for classical network inference leading to further understanding of their complexity. Moreover new quantum technologies could be key to design complex quantum networks in experimental set-up leading to novel quantum phenomena displaying a rich interplay between topology and dynamics. From the dynamical point of view directions that are particularly promising and that lie at the classical/quantum interface are progress on quantum synchronization [138] and on network dynamics dictated by the topological Dirac operator [35]. Finally the full potential of networks as a powerful tool to understand quantum matter is not yet fully explored and provides a very promising direction for unsupervised detection of quantum phase transitions. As we have seen, the field has already produced important contributions in each of its research lines which have so far progressed and evolved mostly independently with some notable exceptions. For example, Hamiltonians derived from a graph can be both simulated with cluster or graph states [192,193] or be used for their adiabatic preparation [292]. The states in turn could be used to replace conventional quantum memories [289] or for error correction in quantum communication networks [533], but for very short distances one may consider state transfer or transport with suitable Hamiltonians again [23,178]. If the communication network could be prepared into a continuous variable cluster state entanglement could then be distributed using the protocol of [254], found to be efficient in particular in sparse complex networks. Finally, networks with comparable complexity to the classical Internet can be constructed even from the ground state of a two dimensional spin lattice by taking as nodes not individual spins but regions of spins of varying sizes and as links entangled clusters of spins shared by exactly two nodes, constituting communication channels [107]. However we believe that there remains much more potential in the ways the lines could further couple together. In the light of the above the interaction between the different research lines and the interdisciplinary collaboration between physicists and network scientists will be key to foster new discoveries in the field and to address the new challenges that the next generation of quantum technologies will require science to face.<fulltext>Original Content from this work may be used under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. title: Normal quantum channels and Markovian correlated two-qubit quantum errors
abstract: We study general 'normally' (Gaussian) distributed random unitary transformations. These distributions can be defined in terms of a diffusive random walk in the respective group manifold. On the one hand, a Gaussian distribution induces a unital quantum channel, which we will call 'normal'. On the other hand, the diffusive random walk defines a unital quantum process, generated by a Lindblad master equation. In the single qubit case, we show different distributions may induce the same quantum channel. In the case of two qubits, we study normal quantum channels, induced by Gaussian distributions in SU ( 2 ) circle times SU ( 2 ) . They provide an appropriate framework for modeling quantum errors with classical correlations. In contrast to correlated Pauli errors, for instance, they conserve their Markovianity, and they lead to very different results in error correcting codes. This is illustrated with an application to entanglement distillation.
text: <title>Normal quantum channels and Markovian correlated two-qubit quantum errors<abstract>We study general 'normally' (Gaussian) distributed random unitary transformations. These distributions can be defined in terms of a diffusive random walk in the respective group manifold. On the one hand, a Gaussian distribution induces a unital quantum channel, which we will call 'normal'. On the other hand, the diffusive random walk defines a unital quantum process, generated by a Lindblad master equation. In the single qubit case, we show different distributions may induce the same quantum channel. In the case of two qubits, we study normal quantum channels, induced by Gaussian distributions in SU(2) ⊗ SU(2). They provide an appropriate framework for modeling quantum errors with classical correlations. In contrast to correlated Pauli errors, for instance, they conserve their Markovianity, and they lead to very different results in error correcting codes. This is illustrated with an application to entanglement distillation.<Introduction>The concept of Gaussian or normally distributed errors is ubiquitous in science and technology, where students are introduced to this concept, in undergraduate courses [1]. The most basic techniques of error estimation in experiments or observations are based on the assumption of a normally distributed error. Surprisingly a similarly flexible and general error model is still missing in the area of quantum communication and quantum computing. Most commonly, error correction protocols, communication protocols, etc are validated against uncorrelated single qubit Pauli errors [2,3]. In the case of uncorrelated single-qubit errors, normal quantum channels (i.e. quantum channels induced by Gaussian distributions) are essentially equivalent to Pauli errors. However, in the case of correlated two-qubit errors this is no longer the case. Correlated qubit errors may arise in quantum communication protocols, where several qubits must be sent in order to perform error correction or entanglement distillation. They also occur in current quantum computing platforms, for instance in the implementation of control-not gates [4,5]. Typically, these two-qubit errors largely dominate the accumulated error in the realization of a given quantum algorithm [6,7]. Early implementations of correlated errors were rather particular models [8,9] and only since very recently they are studied more systematically under the term 'crosstalk errors' [10,11]. Note that such correlated errors can be particularly harmful to fault-tolerant quantum error correction [10]. The modeling, estimation and eventual mitigation of correlated errors faces the problem of a potentially large number of undetermined parameters. For instance, we may reasonably assume a noisy Ctrl-Not gate to be generated from random unitaries in SU (4), which has 15 generators and hence there are about 15 2 parameters to be estimated. The recently developed strategy to deal with this problem consists in 'randomized compiling' [12] in connection with twirling [13][14][15]. In favorable situations, the resulting effective noise channels become diagonal Pauli channels which require only 15 probabilities for their characterization. In such a scheme, the original noisy gate will be mapped into the composition of the ideal Ctrl-Not gate followed by a Pauli-Lindblad noise gate. This may then allow for error mitigation techniques which are quite effective [11,16,17], at least theoretically. However, since quantum computing is realized with a finite number of realizations, the effectiveness of the approach should be estimated within these limits. For doing so Cai et al in [18] define the means square error MSE for a measurement estimator at the end of a quantum circuit, where this estimator is calculated from N cir repetitions (shots). In the simplest case the estimator consists of running the real noisy circuit, including the final measurement of the observable, and performing the average over the N cir repetitions. If we want to predict the MSE for this case, assuming a certain error model (as the one we are discussing in this paper), a quantum channel description or a Lindblad master equation are not enough. One needs to compute variances of the elements of the matrix representation of the quantum channel. The concept of Gaussian distributed errors allows to do exactly this, and it can provide explicit algebraic expressions for these quantities. In this work we use the Gaussian distributions on compact Lie groups as defined in [19,20] to construct models for quantum errors. Such distributions have first been introduced in SO(3) with applications in estimating uncertainties in the orientation of rigid bodies [21,22]. The modeling of quantum errors is based on the idea that during the implementation of a given gate, residual random unitary operations intersperse leading to an effective noisy quantum channel. We show that different distributions can yield the same noisy quantum channel, and we explain how to distinguish between classical and quantum correlations. For illustration, we consider a simple protocol for entanglement distillation and show that in this case, classical correlations are less harmful to error correction than one may have anticipated. Similar error models which include cross talk have been proposed only recently in the form a Markovian Pauli-Lindblad master equations [11]. However, the extra gain of our approach consists in the possibility to consider and calculate higher moments of the respective noisy quantum channel. The paper is organized as follows: After this introduction, in section 2, we present a heuristic derivation for Gaussian distributions on compact Lie groups based on the formal definition from [19,20]. We find an expression that allows us to compute the quantum channel induced by any particular Gaussian distribution. In section 3, we define a general normal channel and derive a Lindblad equation describing its evolution in time, we then describe how to calculate quantum channel fluctuations using the mean square error (MSE). In section 4, we consider the single qubit case. We find a simple correspondence between the Gaussian distributions centered on the identity, and general Pauli channels. Furthermore, we find that for any Lindblad-divisible quantum channel [23], there are one or more Gaussian distributions which generate this channel. In section 5, we study Gaussian distributions in the group SU(2) ⊗ SU(2), to describe random errors in two-qubit operations. By construction, these distributions induce channels which can contain classical correlations, only (this is the main practical difference to Gaussian distributions in SU(4)). In section 6, we illustrate the effect of correlated normal errors in a simple protocol for entanglement distillation. We conclude our paper with section 7.<Gaussian distributions on compact Lie groups>In probability theory, a probability distribution is infinitely divisible if it can be expressed as the probability distribution of the sum of an arbitrary number of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables [24][25][26]. In order to apply this concept to transformation groups, the sum must be replaced by the group operation. In addition, we require a unique invariant probability measure on the group, and we use some tools of harmonic analysis and there in particular the Peter-Weyl theorem. For these reasons, we restrict ourselves to the case of compact Lie groups [27].<General normal quantum channels>For a compact Lie group G with a unitary irreducible matrix representation U(g) = D (s) (g) and Gaussian distribution f parameterized by a diffusion matrix A and a drift vector ⃗ b, we define a general normal quantum channel as where ϱ is a density matrix of finite dimension, related to the parameter s. A case of particular interest will be considered below, in section 4, where U(g) is interpreted as a random unitary operation applied to a single qubit. We remark that we chose the name 'normal' for the channels instead of 'Gaussian' because the term 'Gaussian channels' is already used for quantum channels in continuous variables [31]. In what follows, we derive a Lindblad master equation [32,33], which generates the quantum map Λ(A, ⃗ b ) when integrated over a fixed time interval. To do so, we use the divisibility of f, which implies that for any finite n > 0 there exist a distribution h n such that the ensemble {U} f is indistinguishable from {u n . . . u 2 u 1 } hn . Then, we introduce t = j/n, with 0 ⩽ j ⩽ n and δ = 1/n, to find due to the statistical independence of the {u j }. Thereby, we arrive at the differential equation [33], We use once more the fact that h n is ever more localized at the identity, and insert for u = D (s) (g) the exponential map in equation ( 6), expanding it up to second order, which yields where we have used commutators [ •, • ] and anti-commutators { •, • } to shorten the notation. Thereby we finally arrive at the desired master-equation, In the finite-dimensional case, and for unital quantum processes this is the most general form of a Lindblad master equation, where it is required that A is real and positive semi-definite, and where ⃗ b determines the Hamiltonian of the system [33,34]. For t = 1, we obtain the quantum channel defined in equation (13). For other values t ⩾ 0, we obtain a one-parameter family Λ t of quantum channels, i.e. a quantum process. In view of the construction, it is clear that this process is CP-divisible (i.e. divisible in completely positive and trace preserving maps) in the sense of [35]. In [23], the authors define a quantum channel to be 'Lindblad divisible' (L-divisible), if there exits a Lindblad master equation (with time-independent coefficients) which generates that channel in a finite amount of time. In this sense, normal quantum channels are always Ldivisible, and at the same time, any L-divisible unital quantum channel is normal. This means that any Lindblad master equation can be solved (numerically) by an appropriate diffusive random walk in the corresponding dynamical group. This is precisely the basis of the so called 'quantum state diffusion' method [36][37][38][39]. However it is possible that two different tuples (A, ⃗ b) generate the same quantum channel. We will analyze this situation for the single qubit case in the following section 4.<Single qubit normal quantum channels>Here, we investigate the application of Gaussian distributions for describing imperfect quantum gates acting on single qubits (two-level quantum systems). This means that instead of a fixed unitary transformation U 0 ∈ SU(2), we assume that a random transformation with a Gaussian distribution in SU(2) is applied; see equation (13). The result is a non-unitary quantum operation, i.e. a linear, completely positive and trace-preserving (CPTP) [2] map, or simply a quantum channel, in the space of 2 × 2 density matrices. The special unitary group SU(2) has the Wigner D-matrices D (s) (g) as irreducible representations with s = 0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, . . .. It has r = 3 generators which are the angular momentum operators divided by ℏ. Since we are dealing with qubits, U(g) = D (1/2) (g), where the generators can be written in terms of the Pauli matrices ⃗ L (1/2) = ⃗ σ/2 [40]. The Gaussian distribution f (g) is parameterized by the pair (A, ⃗ b ) (see equation ( 12)).<Two qubit normal channels and correlated errors>In this section we construct normal quantum channels, which can describe correlated noise affecting two-qubit quantum gates in a general, intuitive manner. For that purpose, we consider Gaussian distributions in the group SU(2) ⊗ SU(2) and compare the resulting quantum channels to a model of correlated Pauli errors [8,9].<Application: entanglement distillation>In this section we consider the problem of entanglement distillation where we expect to find significant differences when modeling the transmission errors either with Λ cP (m) (correlated Pauli errors) or Λ c2 (ρ) (normal correlated errors). As a starting point, we consider the protocol introduced in [48,49], where the sender (Alice) has two Bell pairs in the state she wants to share with a receiver (Bob). For that she sends one qubit of each Bell pair through a noisy quantum channel to Bob. At this point, we assume that the qubits are sent together or one after the other through a noisy channel, where they pick up correlated errors. It will be convenient to view this basic distillation protocol as a map from the space of two-qubit quantum channels to the space of density matrices as follows: where Λ E2 is the two-qubit error map. The distillation protocol D is shown in figure 3. Right after the transmission of the two qubits, Alice and Bob apply control-not gates to the two qubits in their possession, and measure σ z in one of those as shown in the diagram. They communicate their measurement results to each other. If their results coincide, they use the remaining qubits as an improved Bell pair, otherwise they discard the qubits and start anew. This requires four Bell pairs at the beginning and yields two independent approximate Bell pairs as a result: where we allow that the error channel applied in the first distillation protocol is different from the one applied in the second. Afterwards, we apply a post-processing protocol Λ post to the two approximate Bell pairs, such that the complete distillation protocol may be expressed as This post-processing protocol is shown in figure 4. It takes the two approximate Bell states resulting from the application of D ⊗2 and first applies Hadamard gates to all the qubits. Then it applies the same process as in D, which results in a single improved Bell state at the end. The protocol D u can fix errors which include the three types σ x , σ y and σ z at the cost of using four Bell states. In the following, we consider the effect of correlations on the efficiency of the distillation process. In doing so, we compare correlated Pauli errors (Λ cP (m)) with correlated normal errors (Λ c2 (ρ)). In both panels, we show the case without distillation with a black solid line. This case is described by equation (67). Note that for p = 1/4, the error channel becomes the completely depolarizing channel, which leaves the pair of qubits shared by Alice and Bob in the uniformly mixed state. Therefore F n (p) = 1 -3p, and F n (1/4) = 1/4. Then we consider the fidelity F u under the distillation protocol D u in the case of uncorrelated errors. Since Λ cP (0) = Λ c2 (0), both cases yield the same result, shown by a single red solid line. As anticipated in equation (68), we see the gain in fidelity for small error probabilities, where the fidelity decay is quadratic in p. Finally, let us discuss the case of maximal correlations. For the correlated Pauli channel Λ cP (1), this means that in figure 3 always the same Pauli errors are applied to qubits 1.k and 2.k. For p = 1/4, D u leaves the two qubits in the state This state contains only classical correlations, and it results in F u = 1/2. In figure 5, panel (a), the result for the correlated Pauli channel is shown by a purple solid line. It ends indeed at F u (1/4) = 1/2. Note that for small values of p, the distillation protocol cannot provide any improvement which is in line with our intuition. Importantly, the situation is very different for the correlated normal channel, Λ c2 (1). Here, small values of p mean that random errors are realized by unitaries which are close to the identity. In that case, even for maximally correlated errors, the distillation protocol is almost as effective as in the uncorrelated case. Figure 6 shows the fidelity of the distillation protocol D u in the case of correlated normal errors, Λ c2 (ρ) as a function of the error probability p, for different values of ρ. We can see that for small values of p the protocol is always very effective, and different values of the correlation coefficient ρ yield very similar results. This changes only at larger values p ≲ 1/4. In this Figure we include two cases with anti-correlated errors ρ < 0, which show that there is no symmetry between positive and negative correlations. For small errors, the correlations decrease the effectivity of the distillation, and the highest fidelity is achieved for ρ = 0.<Conclusions>In this paper we use Gaussian distributions on compact Lie groups to derive explicit expressions for the associated normal quantum channels. This provides a general framework for describing errors in quantum processing devices analogous to normally distributed errors in classical systems. The divisibility of the Gaussian distributions allows us to view them as the result of a diffusive random walk in the group manifold. In the space of quantum channels, this gives rise to a differentiable quantum process, described by a Lindblad master equation. In this framework the relationship between the parameters of the Lindblad equation and those of the Gaussian distribution are particularly transparent. This simplifies the construction of physically reasonable error models. However, the extra gain of our model consists in a more detailed description of the error model. While in some cases this may not be necessary, in others it is of crucial importance. In this sense, we considered the MSE introduced in 3.1, which is a necessary quantifier to evaluate the effectiveness of quantum error mitigation. We show that this quantity can be calculated for normal quantum errors as induced by Gaussian distributions, while for standard error models which are limited to quantum channels and Lindblad master equations, this is not possible. We then focus on the groups SU(2) and SU(2) ⊗2 , which are particularly relevant for quantum information processing with qubits. In the case of SU(2) (single qubit case), we first show that the normal channels are essentially equivalent to Pauli channels, which have always been fundamental to modeling errors in quantum information science. Then, we demonstrate that different Gaussian distributions may be associated to the same normal quantum channel. Intuitively, this can be understood in terms of the diffusive random walk picture. In this picture, different random walks describe different quantum processes, which nonetheless may arrive at the same quantum channel at the correct time. In the case of SU(2) ⊗2 (two qubit case), the Gaussian distributions provide a flexible and intuitive framework for describing correlated quantum errors in the implementation of twoqubit quantum gates, or in the transmission of pairs of qubits across a noisy quantum channel. Choosing here SU(2) ⊗2 over SU(4), amounts to restricting ourselves to single qubit errors with classical correlations. When comparing to other models of correlated errors, our model has the advantage of being Markovian, by definition, of being able to describe a noisy quantum gate as a single object (no separation between ideal quantum gate and posterior noise gate), and naturally separate classical from quantum correlations. For illustration, we consider entanglement distillation in the presence of correlated isotropic single-qubit errors. In this example, we found important differences between the model based on normal channels and the one based on Pauli channels. For a small error rate, normal channels apply small random rotations to the qubits. Then, even in the presence of correlations, the distillation process remains very effective. In the case of classical devices, the method of error propagation is based on the assumption of normally distributed errors. In this way, it provides a simple way to calculate the overall error in a given circuit of error prone operations. It may be possible to develop an analogous method for quantum circuits. Another, may be more important line of research would consist in applying our models to evaluate the effectiveness of quantum error mitigation in realistic settings. That would imply for instance to really evaluate the cost of twirling, assuming that the noisy quantum gate can be modeled as a normal quantum channel with underlying Gaussian distribution. title: The standard symmetrized skew information and its applications
abstract: In this paper, we propose two new measures: one is symmetrized skew information and the other one is standard symmetrized skew information. Firstly, we prove their properties, such as non-negativity, convexity, invariance, additivity, monotonicity and strong monotonicity. Next, we conduct research on relationships between standard symmetrized skew information and several well-known measures in one-qubit state, aiming to compare their similarities and differences. In addition, standard symmetrized skew information is used to study quantum uncertainty. We also give the definition of standard symmetrized skew information of assistance, and provide it a straightforward operational explanation for better understanding. Finally, standard symmetrized skew information can be applied to detect entanglement.
